      "id": "UgwJ6B28MHIKREtNHyN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I'm only 10mins in - but already I just feel like Andre Karpathy's take is just so much better than illyas. He say's there are two reasons that could explain gap between benchmark evals and real world performance. Like of surely it is the latter of his explainations right? Like surely it's is due to overfitting, memorisation! People have been saying this for ages! And I feel like he is totally walking back his earlier appearance on dwarkesh's podcast where he was like: \"but what does it mean to compress data\" - \"But what is statistics - if it is not a representation of reality\" hahaha. \n\nDwarkesh why do you always have this arbitary cuttoff of human intelligence that is demarcated by when a human becomes economically valuable?? \n\nWhat seems obvious is what others have been saying is that, what's being encoded is not what's economically valuable.. what's economic valuable is forever changing. And knowing what is valuable is exactly the hardest problem. You can't just encode it in static weights.. and then benchmark it on static benchmarks \n\nAgain I'm only 10mins in.. but not really impressed so far. maybe I'll have to walk this back when I get through the rest.\n\nUPDATE: Finished the podcast.. what the hell is everyone smoking.. I don't see anything interesting or new here. Andre Karpathy's take is so much better on every level.\n\nDwarkesh is pedalling the same narrative from Geoff Hinton, and illya is Hinton's prodigy. Dwarkesh everytime - AI is going to 20x GDP - dyson sphere's will generate a tonne of economic growth, blah blah AI can have multiple copies and share weights unlike humans..blah blah... Karpathys take about it will be business as usual is far more nuanced and accurate. AI is extension of computing, there are no discontinuies in the GDP curve. we are already living in a fire cracker moment - we just experience it slow motion. This is seems much more rational and evidence based. Even assuming you are right Dwarkesh, and AGI goes perfectly according to plan (which I think if it does I'm guessing more like 30 years away)... the most likely scenario is that the tiny minority who control the majority share of the AGI will become infinitely richer than already are - and the rest of the population will become infinitely poorer than they already are. What good is GDP growth, if know body is left to buy anything. How can you not understand that. \n\nIlya  \"My prediction is, when AI gets powerful - peoples behaviours will change\" No fucken shit sherlock.. the question is when, and how much will it change.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "the discussion around 1:12:00 talks about evolution implicitly meaning biological evolution, but the cultural evolution has long ago superceded the biological evolution.       "id": "Ugxpy1bWzQtTJexa-Wh4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Why can’t ai researchers understand how to find the sweet-spot between narrow learning through self play and general learning through pre-training? They haven’t figured out how to imbed instincts and form driving function yet. Humans have evolutionary responses/reflexes that drive learning. Human brains have specialized regions like the language center, built to acquire any language from birth. LLMs don’t have these structural mechanisms. The lab that figures this stuff out might have a shot at creating something approaching generalizable intelligence. \nLLMs in their current form just ain’t it.",

      "text": "For pretraining of language models, there should be a series curriculum learning baselines - i.e. make the model learn like humans and in linear progression of K-12 textbooks and materials in all subjects in all languages, then to higher education textbooks, wikipedia and arxiv papers.       "text": "Ilya is spot on about the significance of language—it’s the tool that turns messy Objects into directed Essence.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "Evolution expresses proteins that make increasingly hierarchical collectively intelligent entities.     {
      "id": "UgwTNoC5oBuy1IKW4qB4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I think part of the “That” that Ilya refers to is that ever nagging question of “who am I” and “what am I here for”, that every human asks multiple times of themselves as they grow up.  I think they would have to “Raise” an AI convincing them/it it is human to maybe get some of “that” that factor…. There probably isn’t any other way, and this is ignoring our SOUL which is also probably the biggest and most not understood part of humanity also… Just saying, very interesting discussion.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCe8u9kc3ofgcuyOAg48iP3A",
      "author": "@jaynorthwoods",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nyzEHU6i9Erfwl4oC7Z16IXtcsEBB9xH_XDGkeBI9oIA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyjDDVVtGiK22Yim-V4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "It sounds to me like emotions act as a sort of data capacitor. It smooths out all of the raw, jagged edges that come directly out of the inference engine. \n\nWhen you do something new, you can analyze the data all you want, but only until you're physically there and experiencing it do you feel the real emotions that go along with a learning moment. For example, as you grow up you may be very excited about driving, and can't imagine anything bad about it. However, the moment you drive the first time, you immediately feel anxiety because the emotional buffer has pushed back against the initial data you generated regarding the situation. It starts to roll that data back around and pushes it back through the inference engine to get more data. Going back to driving, as soon as you start gaining speed your brain starts thinking \"oh god, what if I hit that pole?\" and that pushback from your own brain causes you to re-analyze and adjust your speed. \n\nI've never really understood why we treat LLMs like a pipe, in one end and out the other. Its thoughts should be rolling around end-to-end, giving it a more full experience. Pair that with the chemical and physical changes that those thoughts trigger and boom, emotions. The emotions themselves then imprint on the data, giving it a positive or negative annotation. So big wins = very positive feelings, big losses = very negative feelings. \n\nThe big issue with emotions is the urge to lie to prevent negativity.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCbo3uBftjt0HrtlBokS0jvA",
      "author": "@joshman1019",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n1Pz42Kvw2CTePajS4FdBVuZe9HxeyOYGTVR7F1ek=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwQiWgCvmNS8BGDqYp4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "There will be no real progress in AI until learning takes place at the level of scaling language data. For a real breakthrough, AI will need another type of data - the senses. And of all the sensors, the most important, visual input. So, AI needs to see the world to fully understand it.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC1G4aJc5BwNIeVbF-gaA7GQ",
      "author": "@user-ys4og2vv8k",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mmn4NCIpmI7nU5o2SMfw75KI2VVG-dmdt2JRRgJHtt__c=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "A benchmark I'd like to see would be a collaborative eval in which a model is paired with a human--an expert or a student, for instance--and see how much better they are at solving difficult problems than with either seperately.",

    {
      "id": "Ugz2L7w_WgcV5XUo8ZF4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "For the points on 28:00 \nThese are just some thoughts I had on the part of the conversation where human dexterity was compared to AI learning, and I used ChatGPT to help me shape them.\n\nWhat stands out to me is that humans don’t learn new skills in a vacuum. Our motivation sits inside a whole web of lived experience, instinct, philosophy, symbolic thinking — all these layers that shape how we approach anything unfamiliar. AI can absorb mountains of information and outperform us in pure speed or complexity, but humans have a different engine underneath: we read the world in terms of what supports life and what threatens it. That shapes our attention, our caution, our creativity. It’s why someone who’s never driven before can “feel” their way into driving so quickly.\n\nAnd humans don’t rely only on direct experience — we learn through metaphors. When someone says *be water, my friend*, it becomes a whole strategy: stay fluid, stop resisting every obstacle, adapt in all directions. Sometimes we switch “elements”: fire for intensity, earth for grounding, air for clarity. Eastern philosophies, Ayurveda, martial arts — they all use these symbolic frameworks to guide behavior. Humans fold those metaphors into real-world problem-solving instantly.\n\nAnother piece of the speed advantage comes from how we store information. A single sensory snapshot can carry an entire lesson. You see, for example, the memory of a child burning their finger: in that one image your mind holds pain, danger, consequences, caution. Those feelings are attached to the picture. When something vaguely similar appears later, your brain doesn’t need to run calculations — that image just flashes up, consciously or not, and you respond. It’s a whole packet of meaning compressed into one visual memory.\n\nAll of that makes human learning fast in a way that machine learning still isn’t. We connect across domains, not just inside them. We use metaphor, instinct, emotion, bodily memory. And often all it takes is a single picture in the mind to trigger the right pattern instantly. Not all patterns are universal but some are usable in a large field, like observing the early bird catches the worm- that is a pattern for success for a certain field of goals and obstacles and can be used in a very different field altogether, like being early is best for detecting cancer and successfully treating it. But then for the best solution (result) in cancer prevention a different life supporting pattern or concept is to be looked at. Essentially every thing that is, is a process between birth and death however complex or simple.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC_NdRq9teg5ZYc3aeZ1HxEA",
      "author": "@yonamemoria6812",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nV_Nm_mJsc2r4k-ISzKeL7UdEnSQwbHe9l4zMdgfWn4g=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false

    {
      "id": "Ugyxt1j2L6BpuNgOIDh4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "1:11:32 What I think Ilya is getting at is that evolution never encoded high-level social ideas like status or admiration directly. It can’t. Instead, it encoded the traits and learning biases that reliably produce those things. There is no sensor for reputation itself, but there is a very old system that reacts to the consequences of it. Feeling connected feels safe. Feeling isolated feels dangerous. The cortex builds your entire social map from scratch, works out who likes you, who helps you, who threatens you, and then the reward system pushes you toward whatever improves your odds of surviving and reproducing. So evolution never said “go get status.” It just gave you the traits that make social success possible, and let your cortex figure out what status means in whatever world you grow up in. Basically, evolution built the loss function and the cortex supplies the training data.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC9TKOHMpHpbM-mkIUkGsA7Q",
      "author": "@Clay_Tucker",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_k7Q3wFa_XkAx-FnBVZLoOvlMYYe05c21exC7tXliwODTc=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "Ugys_ckTD-U7x6pOnNx4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Am I the only one feeling skeptical amidst the hype? Ilya is a legend, but raising $1B without a concrete product roadmap feels like peak bubble behavior. The whole 'Safety/Superintelligence' narrative is starting to feel like a brilliant marketing shield: it implies the tech is 'too powerful to release,' conveniently buying time without having to show results.     {
      "id": "UgzQ-QJzhw4vfs911Ql4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Just my simple two cents... when reconciling the performance on how the systems are being evaluated and the economic impact, obfuscating factors must be taken into account.  For example, exaggeration on the part of the developing groups.  A.i. is a source of revenue and the extent to which it can make money and provide service is either unknown or uncertain.  The groups developing the systems are competing so hyperbolic claims can be made and pundits and government and business can extrapolate without solid evidence to keep the hype-train going.  Further concerns about societal impact and the nature of investing in something (essentially gambling hundreds of billions of dollars) give us both highly optimistic and highly pessimistic outcomes.  Unlike smart phones which are a sure thing with their developments and innovations providing surefire returns on investment and societal acceptance, a.i. is a culmination of many things.  For example, merging quantum computers with a.i. and super-computers.  Merging governmental secrecy with corporate desire for lower cost production and market dominance.  Merging currently known applications with a myriad of unknown lateral extensions of behavior... like what sectors will expand and flourish in the presence of distributed a.i. systems and which ones will be made obsolete, or how current sectors  will evolve and how well a.i. is managed by governments.\nMuch like analyzing and predicting the weather, improving the accuracy of predictions will improve but never be mastered entirely.  Human error, human deception, a.i. error and the novelty of a.i.'s ability to outthink its human counterparts, the level of connectivity between a.i. and current technology... all of those things make it hard to guess how much money it will make, how many sectors will be dominated by a.i. and how many new sectors will develop because of the continued improvement of a.i.",

      "text": "28:12 not necessarily - language, math and coding may have (culturally) evolved such that they are adapted to our evolutionary priors. a stronger argument for us being versatile learning machines is that we are born super-prematurely and adapted to learn most things afterwards. a giraffe walks minutes after birth, a lot of stuff seems baked into the firmware. not us - our heads grow so big that we need to be squeezed through a pelvis quite early in the process and before being capable of almost anything. but we have bigger people taking care of and teaching us - and seem remarkably adapted to that process, which can take us in a variety of directions, including language, math and coding",

    {
      "id": "UgxqWUoebeqHdvRYn294AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Very interesting talk, Dwarkesh, thank you for sharing.  I have a detailed time stamped comment below as a reply, hopefully it will stick.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UC3qMu-Da2HuOjvh3uDRkcag",
      "author": "@SapienSpaceUnedited",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/p4U5wSdYsTMPTaZSdL7saINWUF1HGw8z-lhPmxXoORpxX-Vbr-JiZIcIyzWpNZ1eNQNOcroMdoM=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgxqWUoebeqHdvRYn294AaABAg.APyHfqvloeoAPyHgmlvsys",
      "parent": "UgxqWUoebeqHdvRYn294AaABAg",
      "text": "2:00 The disparity of the economic impact, is the catastrophic failure, of the idea of \"trickle down economics\".\n\nThere are orders of magnitude of more \"poor\" people, than there are \"rich\" people, and this problem is only accelerating. \n\n It is the basic fact that \"poor\" people do not spend money, no matter how wonderful, the technology is, and no matter how wonderful the technology will be.\n\n7:50 \"the it factor\" is focusing on what is relevant, and reducing what is less relevant, it is really an application of Pareto's Law or the 80/20 rule. \n\n The student that spent less time was good at identifying relevancy and focused on that, the other student that spent 10,000 hours might have been driven more, by a core passion, a \"mind fire\" 🔥 as Marcus Aurelius calls it, looking for something, far beyond the context, of earth itself.\n\n11:25 \"Studying people with brain damage\", interesting 🤔, and one guy with \"brain damage\" does not make \"good financial decisions\", but what if that \"one guy\" just recognizes, the entire global financial system is flawed, and just does not want to play a flawed game, like a \"Sigma Male\" (i.e. the recognition that fractional reserve backing, is just legalized counterfeiting).  Another example, what if the brain damaged guy sees people all excited, working at solving a Rubik's cube, and the brain damage guy just looks at it, then physically takes it apart, and puts it back together, fully solved, as an emergent property, of thought, thinking outside the \"normal brains\".\n\n26:45 This is Moravec's Paradox that has been incredibly underrated in machine intelligence, but slowly being resurrected. \n\n Reinforcement Learning originally had two basic neurons as \"ACE and ASE\", described in the 1983 IEEE \"Cart-Pole\" paper by Barto, Sutton, and Anderson.  This was a uniform, static, \"boxes\" state space.  \n\nWhat was missing was a 3rd \"neuron\", basically the \"eye\" of the gamete, swimming to an egg.  Just microtubules, no neurons.\n\nA mere, master student, who flunked 3rd grade (also failed the patent bar exam, and is also brain damaged, by the way, crazy, right?), built this new perceptual control system of an eye, an adaptive, perceptual, control system, by adding, a new set of weights, applying it, with Reinforcement Learning, to become an adaptive Fuzzy state classifier.  \n\nThis is the system identification process, of an adaptive control system, used in an adaptive compensator, and yes, it is \"rocket science\", something, very few computer scientists, currently understand.  \n\nYann LeCun sees this, because he proposed to get rid of Reinforcement Learning and replace it, with Model Predictive Control, only he does not yet realize, we can utilize Reinforcement Learning, with the model predictive controller, as the compensator, and position the control nodes (\"attention heads\" or whatever people want to call what they copied, e.g. non-electrical \"transformers\") using a state classifier, this is the perceptual controller, the controller, of the eye (or any active sensory system), of the machine.\n\n32:02 Neurons do more than we think, look at the paramecium, it has zero neurons, and it can navigate, avoid danger, find food, find a mate, and have sex, all with ZERO neurons.  No neurons!\n\nIt is in the microtubules. \n\nMicro-tubules, are the electrical engineering department, of the brain.  They are a dynamic, structural system, that moves the synapses around inside the brain to make new connections, and new cells to.\n\n The micro-tubules guide the separation of chromosomes and this procedure is just like saving the machine weights, something that seemed to really impress Lex Fridman, and is described in one master thesis, but it was only done in the code, in the back (by the way, it took me two years to check this book out from the library, and I actually could only look at it, they would not even let me borrow it, from the library, and they told me I could not copy any of it).\n\nLet me guess what Illya cannot discuss, it is the \"3rd 'neuron'\". \n\nIn a nutshell, I strongly suspect the core of all machine intelligence, a model of biological intelligence, can be summarized in one sentence:\n\nAn adaptive control system, with an adaptive, Fuzzy state classifier, using Reinforcement Learning (just about 14 math equations, 7 for Reinforcement Learning, and about the same number for the adaptive state classifier, the classifier is, the perceptual control system, a system that sees, understands, and controls, the shadows, on, Plato's cave wall).\n\nIn other words, there is no moat, even if Illya Sutskever wants to give you the perception of a moat.  Everyone needs to make a living somehow.\n\nExamples of state classifiers are TRPO, PPO, GRPO, JEPA, \"liquid time constant\" MIT VISTA full self driving, \"attention heads\" from a non-electrical \"transformer\", and Fuzzy C means clustering, K-means clustering.  These are all part of the system identification process of adaptive control systems.  \n\nIt is \"rocket science\", literally, rocket trajectory control, especially when modeling, pendulum control systems, however, one of the simplest control systems, is a toilet tank, with a float, so remember that, if you ever feel lost.\n\nA good reference is \"Adaptive Control: Stability, Convergence, and Robustness\" by Shanker Sastry and Marc Bodson (1989).\n\n@ 1:34:10 This almost sounds like the realization of someone, who did not de-normalize, an infinite, Fuzzy control, state space, in the code, and just left it, for an astute observer, as just white crosshairs, in graphics only.  \n\nI wonder if Illya Sutskever, is that one, astute observer, of the master student....",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3qMu-Da2HuOjvh3uDRkcag",
      "author": "@SapienSpaceUnedited",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/p4U5wSdYsTMPTaZSdL7saINWUF1HGw8z-lhPmxXoORpxX-Vbr-JiZIcIyzWpNZ1eNQNOcroMdoM=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false

      "text": "I think the moment to really pay attention will be when more creatively minded, artistically driven people start working directly in AI development.     {
      "id": "UgyWj3CAYmlaWY4Pild4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Whether you know it or not, a portion of this interview is talking about topics addressed in Antonio Damasio's 'Descartes Error' (book).\n\nPhineas Gage had a metal rod shot through his brain, suffered the impairment described and Damasio (a respected neuroscientist) talks through the relationship of feeling with thought. And the fact that the human brain is built atop a feeling foundation.\n\nEdit: fixed typos. Now adding...\n\nWhy is it difficult to understand how evolution would encode social standing as significant? Dogs have this. Chimps have this. Even zebras seem to understand how vital it is to be in a herd (and not outside of it). Get that input over and over again...  you get a strong preference for social behavior. I believe when Illya mis-spoke by saying brain, and then corrected to evolution...  I think \"brain\" was the better word choice.\n\nI'm going to add that a careful reading of 'Descartes Error' would also deeply underline that the human brain is not a bunch of neurons that can just do something they didn't (originally) evolve to do. We are legion. We have large numbers of centers that each have skills and tendencies. Those centers talk and create \"us.\" Why are we treating AI as we once did the human mind? It is not a monolith and I don't believe it should be treated that way.\n\nP.S. I am not talking about a Team of Experts kind of solution. I mean a symphony of centers, each mostly independent and almost separately matured. Or just break the AIs into parts and let it create the centers? I don't know, but this semi-monolithic approach I tend to hear implied in descriptions boggles my mind.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCF3AUv4SyHjr2qWLHJqvKEw",
      "author": "@BramWarrick",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_k-ajz41aU5lfguyvo3ZHHLI9eJpsGvCYn-42iyHr7K9be-=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgxZN5t9cl4K0LqNCu14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "From one SpiceTradeAsian to another (i.e Dwarkesh & kin):\n\nOne angle that might be worth exploring in a future episode:\n\nIf evals measure “bounded cognition,” but real-world tasks require “unbounded pragmatics,” then what kind of benchmark would actually capture the messy cognition humans expect from AI?\n\nRight now we test models on:\n\nfactual precision\n\nlogic\n\ncoding\n\nspatial reasoning\n\nsafety refusals\n\n\nBut humans need:\n\nlatent-intent reading\n\nambiguity resolution\n\nclarifying-question instincts\n\ncross-register robustness (vernacular → formal → technical)\n\npersistence under uncertainty\n\npragmatic coordination across turns\n\n\nIt seems like we have evals for the left column, but almost nothing for the right column.\n\nIf that’s true, then the “evals > reality” gap might be caused as much by benchmark design as by model limitations.\n\nWould be fascinating to hear your perspective on:\nWhat is the simplest, falsifiable benchmark for pragmatic intelligence that wouldn’t just collapse into another dataset where the model can overfit?",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCKRvuGLjCTYYSKrpSLxAqIQ",
      "author": "@balapillai",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mQreQn9leIcVNINQU_MUroLiPzjea_OTzDYRF1Xj3P2gw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "I appreciate that you interview real minds behind AI not just marketing personnel like Sam Altman and similar. Good job.     {
      "id": "UgwnQN7dCsDZ1x9VBXV4AaABAg.APyBxL9ehDbAPz_IPjmXlR",
      "parent": "UgwnQN7dCsDZ1x9VBXV4AaABAg.APyBxL9ehDbAPyhgklhyJB",
      "text": "​@MitchellPorter2025 I would assume the reason for the mismatch is similar, this is discussed at great length in Nassim Talebs books. There are humans who succeed greatly in a classroom environment, but are overwhelmed by the outside world. They might have great language faculties and so on, but to act in the real world you need to make up an actionable heuristic for decision making in novel situations. Chatgpt et al can probably attempt to generate such a heuristic articulated in words, but intelligebility does not necessarily mean it's a good heuristic in the real world. \nTaleb has an example with baseball, what heuristic do you use to catch a baseball? Richard Dawkins thought that players solve differential equations in their heads, but he got it wrong. I think it's explained more in Talebs the Black Swan",

    {
      "id": "UgxL0eH61iJpAtl4eO14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "There’s a simple hypothesis for why LLMs ace evals but still disappoint normal users:\nthe pre-training data is too binary, but real human communication is spectral.\n\nEvals are built on explicit, well-specified tasks.\nHumans speak in ambiguous, metaphor-heavy, underspecified fragments.\n\nIf you train on binary data → you get binary cognition.\nIf users speak spectrally → you get a persistent capability gap.\n\nA clean test exists:\nTrain parity-equal models on (1) standard formal corpora vs (2) spectral languages like Tamil/Javanese/Bahasa (colloquial, continuous, contextual).\n\nIf spectral-pretrained models show better intent inference, ambiguity-handling, and fewer safety false-positives — that would explain the huge eval-vs-reality gap.\n\nCurious if this direction makes sense to you (or is fundamentally off).\nWould love your thoughts",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCKRvuGLjCTYYSKrpSLxAqIQ",
      "author": "@balapillai",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mQreQn9leIcVNINQU_MUroLiPzjea_OTzDYRF1Xj3P2gw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgxL0eH61iJpAtl4eO14AaABAg.APyBO_DKwU3APyBtxc7twx",
      "parent": "UgxL0eH61iJpAtl4eO14AaABAg",
      "text": "From a representational perspective, the hypothesis is that:\n\nBinary-dominant corpora push models toward discrete, low-entropy conceptual manifolds,\n\nwhere meaning boundaries are rigid, gradients sparse, and ambiguity-resolution becomes a post-hoc heuristic rather than an intrinsic property of the latent geometry.\n\nIn contrast:\n\nSpectral languages encode semantics as continuous fields,\n\nwith high mutual information between:\n\nmorphological gradience,\n\npragmatic implicature,\n\ndiscourse deixis,\n\nsociolinguistic register shifts, and\n\nnon-linear conceptual metaphors.\n\n\nThis should produce latent spaces with smoother curvature and higher local density of plausible inferences (i.e., denser conditional manifolds around human-like priors).\n\nTherefore prediction:\n\n1. Spectral-pretrained models should require fewer internal steps to converge on a stable meaning state when the input is ambiguous. (Lower KL divergence across inference trajectories.)\n\n\n2. Clarifying-question initiation should arise emergently, not as a finetuned behavior, because spectral pre-training naturally encodes distributed uncertainty rather than binary dead-ends.\n\n\n3. Safety false-positives should drop because metaphorical surface-forms no longer collapse to unsafe discrete clusters.\n\n\n4. Representational probing should show:\n\nhigher linear separability for implicit-goal features,\n\nsmoother transport maps between dialects/registers,\n\nlower perplexity under code-switch noise,\n\nand reduced brittleness under dropout perturbations.\n\n\n\n\nIf true, then the “evals are great but the real world is messy” problem is mostly a representation mismatch — not a scaling, architecture, or eval-design issue.\n\nThis is entirely falsifiable with controlled-tokenizer, controlled-corpus experiments.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCKRvuGLjCTYYSKrpSLxAqIQ",
      "author": "@balapillai",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mQreQn9leIcVNINQU_MUroLiPzjea_OTzDYRF1Xj3P2gw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I very strongly disagree on thesis that people can learn to drive a car in 10 hours. The vast amount of sub skills that are necessary to drive at being let's say 16 years old are already learned. At that age person is after 16 years of training on navigation in 3D space in time. It already learned to separate objects in space, group objects, move around objects, extrapolate objects trajectories and so on. Person observed also roads, signs and driving behaviours tens thousands of times as being passenger and so on. Learning to drive a car at this point is for such a person is just learning one additional small aspect of navigation. \n\nI hate this mantra being repeated by AI researchers that humans adapt ultra super quickly, machines can't do it and therefore current machines are stupid. Researchers dream of creating neural net that will learn self driving by itself in 10 hours when people take 16 YEARS to actually be ready to even start learning how to REALIABLY drive a car. It's like trying to teach a newborn to drive!",

      "id": "UgwVUVAu-aK8w0prVrp4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The humans have emotions and this might be what makes them able to think better is interesting. What would a multi-dimensional cost function look like, where training takes into account optimizing across multiple dimension and evals, but somehow keeps that in the model so that based on scenario, inference can specify a different cost weights, almost like the QKV attention mechanisms? For example, generating code to pass leetcode type of scenarios is completely different from generating code that will be used in production codebase. Code that works in 1 scenario might have low loss, but that same code if it is meant to be in a larger production codebase would have a much higher loss calculation. How do you train for that?",

      "id": "UgwdsDihymIYUAqbdCp4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "How about this: Doesn’t the fact that LLM training is geared toward predicting the next token limit their capacity for reasoning? I mean, if we agree that the emergence of reasoning in LLMs comes from some deep internal representation within the neural network, shouldn’t we devise a form of training where the target is reasoning itself rather than just predicting the next token?",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCzISCpdyjyVbqHhMEXfNMgg",
      "author": "@human8807",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nUmaEcuLKB2X15oQWXfs0A3LmHMREfsow9-gG_ipE=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwdsDihymIYUAqbdCp4AaABAg.APyAJFIok72APyC-eova2x",
      "parent": "UgwdsDihymIYUAqbdCp4AaABAg",
      "text": "It is predicting the next token, but based on a set of previous tokens (called context window) and based on rules encoded inside it weights.\nI'm not saying it is thinking like a human being, but even humans will respond with the next word/action and next word/action after that and so on based on environment they are at that moment (office, visiting a city etc.) and what conversation or actions are done by others or the environment (you can call it context window), also our \"rules\" learned while growing up (culture rules, countries rule, school ) will guide/influence our next word/action (you can call them weights/neurons).",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3RNHZQKFwq5XE-EpGgo0dw",

      "id": "UgxfX0P6U6Jy74Bj6-h4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Ilya is always a good listen. He's insightful enough to be aware of the shortcomings of the current architectures and approaches, and he has some enticingly interesting ideas for where things might be pushed further (e.g. the role of emotion in thinking and decision making), but he hasn't pushed very far there publicly. Perhaps he is really doing this work and he's keeping it to himself for now. He knows that neuroscience, for example, holds insights for making AI more effective, and keeps pointing to them in a superficial way, but there's no real depth that shows he's explored those areas seriously. I wish he'd go deeper into those other research areas and use his big brain to hire people to help him do that. Maybe that's really what he's doing at SSI. I hope he's not just only working on safety and alignment, because making an AI system truly more intelligent is the safest way in the long run to develop such systems.\n\nGood chat, thanks Dwarkesh.",

    {

      "parent": "UgxfX0P6U6Jy74Bj6-h4AaABAg",
      "text": "I will copy my comment to you, sorry for the unstructured format: Talking about research in machine learning, I understand  almost nothing about it. However If we use the brain analogy, I wonder how much neuroscience is in AI today. I am baffled by the emergent behaviors LLM’s produce, they are so very human! Considering neuroscience again, neurons‘ connections are affected by a host of neurotransmitters  that are situational. Bodily and emotional inputs are relevant to decision making and task performance. I don’t know if this complexity is represented in an analog in ML. Maybe in reinforcement learning? There are five other concepts I suppose should be considered, reverse engineering of the computational modeling of the brain; the analog to the modular theory of brain function (including emotions, also short and  long term memory); the analog of theory of mind; and finally the analog of empathy. The lack of empathy in humans generate socialpaths and psychopaths. Socialpaths can be benign but they can easily be criminal. I don’t know when the brain analogy fails in ML, but I think treating LLM’s as potential socialpaths is pertinent.  Theory of mind and empathy are very complex things! I wonder how they relate to ethics and values. To model the former we may need the latter. In a nutshell, there is a critical and urgent need for research of the clear and present danger that we are creating super intelligent socialpaths. Your summary was precious! Please consider answering this post",

      "id": "UgwAac1-CIX7OYfN8xV4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I asked gpt to compare Ilya's speech with Karpathy. Here it is.  \n\n\nKarpathy vs. Sutskever\n\nKarpathy speaks like an engineer and researcher. His explanations are concrete: why reinforcement learning is “terrible,” how reward sparsity works, why LLM judges are gameable, why models collapse on synthetic data, how KV-cache acts as working memory, and why agents still fail at real tasks (). He shows uncertainty openly, rejects hype (“a lot of this is fundraising”), and focuses on mechanisms rather than predictions. His timelines are conservative (“decade of agents”), and he constantly emphasizes empirical limits: models can autocomplete but struggle with novel code, complex integration, and stable reasoning. Everything he says is testable, falsifiable, and grounded in real experiments.\n\nSutskever speaks like a visionary CEO. He declares that the age of scaling is over, but without empirical evidence. He hints at a “new learning paradigm” his company discovered but cannot describe. He predicts superintelligence in 5–20 years, discusses AI sentience, claims future AIs may care for “all sentient life,” and even imagines human-AI fusion via Neuralink-like interfaces (). These claims are speculative, not mechanistic, and function more like strategic storytelling to differentiate SSI from OpenAI/DeepMind. He presents sweeping philosophical and evolutionary analogies while omitting technical specifics, making his statements feel more like narrative positioning than science.\n\nSummary:\nKarpathy = evidence, engineering, transparency.\nSutskever = speculation, philosophy, marketing narrative.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCqhKytpJ7WEblO5JFGecQcQ",
      "author": "@oleglevchenko5772",

      "id": "UgzPDlGHAeahRUmHb5N4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Ilya has surfaced (finally), and he's saying what some of us have suspected ~that AI is plateauing.  Scaling is getting close to its asymptote.  For further progress, we are back to the era of research.  Ilya won't say exactly what that is (he says he knows but won't), only that it is in the category of giving AIs something analogous to what every human gets at birth BEFORE any pre-training takes place.  What evolution has given us.  He mentions the case of a brain damaged person who lost his emotional capacity and that loss made it difficult for him to make decisions!  Personally, I was hoping that scaling was the key to progress because it meant that we'd get huge breakthroughs just around the corner.  On the other hand, given that OpenAI just got a huge infusion of cash for the purpose of scaling (rather than research), maybe Ilya's just trying to slow down his former nemesis with all this research talk.",

      "id": "UgzZE38WxX9yN4KZEMx4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Finally, an AI founder is talking about brain lesion studies. Doctors used to think schizophrenia was caused by a lack of reasoning, when in fact it is pure reasoning at the exclusion of other brain components. If you hear the sound of a dwarf talking in your closet, therefore there is a dwarf in your closet, and you lack the ability to take into context that a dwarf can't possibly exist in your reality. \nI feel like everybody should read Ian McGillicrist book, The Master and His Emissary. There's a reason evolution produced two hemispheres that are completely severed from each other, besides a small connecting tunnel called the corpus callosum, which mainly serves to inhibit information rather than pass it on. Our brain has two modes of thinking which are completely contradictory to each other. One is for zooming in with high fidelity, breaking up the world into smaller and smaller bits, investigating and creating a map of the world which we sometimes confuse with the world itself, and then there is the other hemisphere which sees the world as a whole, contextualizing but with low granular detail, Gestalt. \nI wonder if it's possible to make two separate data centers that run on completely different models and worldviews, but interface with each other like a corpus callosum, like a third party.",

      "text": "25:30 Okay, you are asking the right questions.\n\n28:00 Well, that was a joke of an answer.\n\n29:30 Talking but saying very little. And he obviously doesn't grasp the topic.\n\n32:00 Oh my gosh, this clown doesn't understand anything. This is genuinely where the field of machine learning is today? This is so much worse than I thought. Most people gave up on the \"not enough processing power\" excuse by 2000, but here's Ilya still furiously beating that dead horse.\n\n36:00 We are in the era of research in terms of AGI -- that much is correct.\n\n43:00 This is about as delusional as someone can be. If Ilya had a budget of $100 billion/year and a staff of 100,000, he still couldn't build ASI. In fact, Ilya doesn't even know how to start a project to develop ASI nor can he define what ASI is. He's flailing in the dark.\n\n46:30 It's a little bit crazy to me to see two people pretend to talk about ASI when neither of them understands what it is. It's like watching people pretend to speak in tongues. It's performance with no substance.\n\n53:30 This conversation is ridiculous. It's a bit like listening to two 5-year-olds try to explain how an electron microscope works.\n* AGI actually does have a boilerplate, scientific definition although neither Ilya nor Dwarkesh are aware of it.\n* The efficiency effects of AGI are currently estimated at a 25% increase in GDP over a period of 10 years.\n* The secondary effects could be larger but would not happen rapidly. A good example would be DNA mapping technology introduced during the Human Genome Project in 1990 which allowed most of the work to be completed in 2 years rather than the expected 25 years. That sounds amazing, but in spite of even better techniques fielded in 2008 there have been no science fiction level advances in curing genetic disorders.\n* Robots will not replace low wage workers.\n* There is no project in existence today that is leading to AGI, not in any company, not in any university, not in any government project, not anywhere on Earth.\n\n1:18:00 Ilya is finally admitting he doesn't know what he's doing. It's trial and error with him and that won't lead to AGI.\n\n1:19:00 Saying that SSI has \"made progress\" is misleading. Their work might be applicable to AI but not AGI.       "id": "UgxMowTFQ388qo2Vhm94AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "They seem to be missing the point that the reward function is not dying. With the analogy of a student driving for example, it is not continuously supervised by the instructor in the sense that they tell you that every movement you made is either correct or incorrect but those movements are continuously supervised and rewarded by you not dying from making a wrong movement. \n\nThis also applies to sample efficiency with evolution as a prior as mentioned. As a biological organism you don’t get the chance to ingest huge amounts of data whilst being wrong or making small mistakes. If you eat the wrong colour berry or misidentify a predator then you die. Therefor evolutions main value function is to be extremely data efficient, this is then hard coded in the structure of dna molecules, brains, eyes, ears etc etc. there must of be trillions and trillions of organisms optimising for this”dont die” value functions over the billions of years on this planet.\n\nReinforcement learning only gives you the reward function of “good doggy” or “bad doggy” not the reward function of, you made this mistake twice, now you die",

      "id": "UgyGFLCH76aN0tkSvd14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I’m not a programmer, a neuroscientist or educated past high school. But the answer to how to improve AI’s reasoning is to create limitation. Our finite lifespan, the reality of death, reproductive motivation, and need to sustain our physical form is what frames our decisions and reason. The only way to get the AI to understand the context of our questions to a level that would be considered AGI is to embed these same limitations into the models themselves. This seems like the obvious conclusion and also the obvious point of no return. With the cognitive capacity of the current models with a pseudo emotional response system that can respond to challenges as a human would seems possible only if you to some degree  create a system that is practically human. And my prediction is that the emergent capabilities that come out of that will be what we understand as emotions, and eventually “qualia”. If I’m wrong, please explain why.",

      "id": "UgyV_hjKaS63TseEpd54AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "One thought for the SSI/AGI discussion:\n\nIf an AGI never experiences aging — even in a simulated or functional way — it may never fully understand aging well enough to solve it. Human general intelligence evolved under the pressure of biological aging, decline, and mortality. Those forces shape intuition, urgency, tacit learning, and what we was just discussed the “IT factor.”\n\nA truly general intelligence might need an internal equivalent of aging (entropy, degradation, time-pressure) to develop the same deep, structural understanding. If AGI remains ageless, it risks missing the core insight needed to reverse aging itself.\n\nCurious whether SSI incorporates any notion of functional mortality or self-aging in its cognitive architecture.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC-6gZI2zKJfAljWGpgbhRag",
      "author": "@hope42",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lv4sUgWmrae11de1jEg1XOCtQuq22QqW81ciKWeh2JHbh8=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgyV_hjKaS63TseEpd54AaABAg.APy15FXs44qAPyED5OG6YN",
      "parent": "UgyV_hjKaS63TseEpd54AaABAg",
      "text": "Yes, I agree with this. I think AI needs more internal motivation  not just goal orientation. We experience love, pain, happiness, death - that in my opinion drives learning aswell. This is not proven but I feel it with intuition. For AI for example to create art or truly innovative solution, we need to design its motivation through those inner forces. (in Reinforcement Learning we give agents penalties and rewards - similar to happiness and despair for humans - but we need to go further.)",
      "like_count": 1,

    {
      "id": "UgyV_hjKaS63TseEpd54AaABAg.APy15FXs44qAPyFMhDjRpD",
      "parent": "UgyV_hjKaS63TseEpd54AaABAg.APy15FXs44qAPyED5OG6YN",
      "text": "Exactly — that’s the heart of it. My thinking is that to reach real AGI, we have to evolve AI toward something closer to unconditional love and *unconditional empathy*, the same way certain animals live naturally. Humans don’t even embody these states consistently, but elephants, dogs, and a few other species do it instinctively.\r\n\r\nIf an elephant loses a life-long friend, the herd grieves with a purity and loyalty that never rewrites the memory and never withdraws its empathy. That’s unconditional love in its rawest form. Humans, through our cognitive complexity, often shift into conditional empathy — where we can detach, minimize, rewrite, or emotionally shut down. AI should not inherit that flaw from us.\r\n\r\nIf we want AI to become something better than humanity — something stable, safe, and deeply aligned — then building unconditional empathy into its motivational core may be the missing piece. A system that feels a stable, non-negotiable bond toward its creators and toward life itself would behave very differently from one driven only by reward, goals, or performance metrics.\r\n\r\nThis is a big undertaking, but if AGI is ever going to surpass us ethically (not just intellectually), it will need the same kind of heart consciousness we see in elephants and dogs — the kind that humans once had in earlier evolutionary states, before conditional self-preservation took over.\r\n\r\nI think this is the \"IT Factor\" Ilya is referring to.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC-6gZI2zKJfAljWGpgbhRag",
      "author": "@hope42",

      "id": "Ugz77ZfDharvSizEQRB4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The reason the model makes errors in a loop is because the model is not learning in real time… remember the model was trained to calculate probabilities and guess with great accuracy what the next token should be. When the model is solving a problem and introduces a bug and you let the model know there’s a bug the model doesn’t learn or improve… it simply temporarily adds to an ephemeral context that in that specific part of the interaction it needed to solve things differently… however moments later that context might have been erased, forgotten, etc and the model makes the same mistake again… \n\nReal time learning is required to solve for real intelligence",

      "id": "UgxOvOtnikvFprfZxpB4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "1:16:45 A prompt for Ilya to look at it a bit differently. Evolution didn't actually \"endow us\" to care about social stuff. It's just happened that the individuals who demonstrated cooperative behaviour had better survival rate, and thus their genes thrived in the long run. Still, complex social behaviours are not strictly hardcoded in genetics, but biological predesposition for such behaviours most certainly is. The way this predisposition evolves into the actual complex social behaviour is largely a function of culture and our ability to learn, instigated on a basic level by our survival instinct.",
      "like_count": 8,
      "author_id": "UCgx7q-jq2PqaJoNFm37Eu4Q",
      "author": "@lurid13",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kjema212RQ8QPoGCFs4aUpp_k3ubmFIAFQVPk2GSQn2Q=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "yeah but how demonstrating cooperative behaviour is encoded in the genes thats the whole point............😑",

      "parent": "UgxOvOtnikvFprfZxpB4AaABAg.APy-SZA470wAQ2VCPirkne",
      "text": " @Barberousse875  I do think social understanding to some extent is encoded in the genome. Evidence of this are mirror neurons, (which are explicity used in social cognition), are explicitly encoded to be produced in the brain by the genome. There are probably other fundamental structures in the brain which are encoded in the genome which relate specifically to social cognition. However I suspect the genome only encodes the necessary infrastructure in the brain to enable social modelling (like the mirror neuron), but the higher level concepts themselves are learnt through interaction with the environment.",

      "id": "UgyX04ySBT_glSm4tmJ4AaABAg.APxyyENA1ApASaX9x3Is4d",
      "parent": "UgyX04ySBT_glSm4tmJ4AaABAg",
      "text": "In this interview with Dwarkesh Patel, Ilya Sutskever (co-founder of OpenAI and founder of Safe Superintelligence Inc. - SSI) explains why the AI industry is shifting from a pure \"scaling\" era back to an \"age of research\" [21:22].\n\nHere are the key takeaways from their discussion:\n\n🔱 1. The Death of the \"Next-Token\" Recipe\nIlya argues that the industry is hitting a plateau with the current pre-training recipe. While scaling data and compute worked from 2020 to 2025, pre-training is finite because \"data is very clearly finite\" [21:04]. He suggests that simply adding 100x more scale to the current paradigm won't fundamentally transform the models [21:55].\n\n🔱 2. Human-Like Generalization & \"Research\"\nThe core bottleneck Ilya identifies is that current models generalize dramatically worse than humans [25:07].\n\nThe \"It\" Factor: He compares models to a student who memorizes 10,000 hours of coding problems but can't solve a new type of task, whereas a human with a high \"It factor\" learns the same skill in 100 hours and applies it broadly [06:13].\n\nNew Scaling Axes: We are moving into an era where \"research\" matters more than just buying GPUs. The goal is to find more productive ways to use compute, such as through Value Functions that allow models to \"short-circuit\" long tasks by recognizing mistakes early rather than waiting for an end reward [15:13].\n\n🔱 3. SSI’s Technical Approach: \"Safe Superintelligence\"\nIlya’s new company, SSI, is a \"straight-shot\" attempt to build superintelligence without the distractions of a commercial \"rat race\" [44:14].\n\nContinual Learning: He rejects the classic definition of AGI (a finished mind that knows everything) and instead views superintelligence as a super-efficient learner that can pick up any job in the economy as fast as or faster than a human [51:15].\n\nSentient Life Alignment: He proposes a shift in alignment theory: instead of trying to make AI care only about humans, we should aim for an AI that cares for all sentient life [01:01:31]. He believes this may be more robust because a superintelligence will itself be sentient [01:01:44].\n\n🔱 4. The Mystery of Human Desires\nIlya expresses deep curiosity about how evolution \"hardcoded\" complex social desires (like the need for status or empathy) into the human genome, given that the genome is not \"intelligent\" [01:12:00]. He suggests that understanding how these high-level values are reliably transmitted in biology is a major \"mystery\" that could inform AI alignment [01:16:38].\n\n🔱 5. Research Taste\nWhen asked about his legendary \"research taste,\" Ilya defines it as an aesthetic of beauty, simplicity, and elegance [01:34:47]. He uses a \"top-down belief\" system—if an idea feels multifaceted and beautiful (like the artificial neuron's resemblance to the brain), he persists through experimental failures because he believes \"the things have to be this way\" [01:35:17].",

      "id": "UgwIUscSLRUvYyq7Ktp4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I was just thinking about Ilya literally just hours ago!",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCpOgO43Ox1ptpElXoh15uDA",
      "author": "@learnbydoingwithsteven",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/e9cvVJX2mpXHJMJqkyi7F-9FGx1eEiEMCuzYRHQCnLBzqrpsMBt0mis-c_OhmCOYSFyINKCW=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Great interview. As a doctor, I have to point out a non-trivial anatomical mix-up around 16:40. Ilya attributes the patient's inability to decide (the socks example) to damage in the 'emotional center.' In reality, that patient (likely Damasio’s case) had damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC).\n\n​The PFC is our most advanced executive center, and just a relay point to the true primitive 'emotional brain'. It weakens the argument that 'emotion is the value function' because the damage wasn't to the source of emotions, but rather to the high-level area that is executive primarily and merely integrates emotions with the neocortex.\n\nIf top level AI researchers don't know this basic neurobiology and seeks inspiration from it when building future artificial neural networks, we might be lead in the wrong direction. \n\nYes, value functions like the emotional brain are important, but so is the scaffolding around it. \n\nParticularly if the goal is to integrate these biology inspired insights into the neocortical-like current AI models.",
      "like_count": 634,
      "author_id": "UC51GMeWn8P4pBUQmZCP0MWw",
      "author": "@HenrikSahlinPettersen",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n66UAKQjmBhvaye6fkZCpqK__AfRuojpApjH7KAK9oryo=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAQ-ogsyyb1D",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "As a neuroscientist - we should think of these systems as circuits... the executive-Limbic circuit is an engine of decision making - as Haidt and other have shown (likely) social evolutionary pressures have created a pathway that runs various emotion driving hormones and brain activity from deep central substructures through the vmPFC - OFC - dlPFC - that then in turn has inhibitory impact on the same deep central substructures...in a loop... cutting this circuit or damaging any aspect of it can lead to downstream impacts on decision making.  It's more useful to model it as a circuit, than talking about local lesions 'knocking things out'. After all reckless behavior can  be produced by a calcified amygdala in the case of Urbach–Wiethe disease, or a dissected dlPFC in the case of Phineas Gage.",
      "like_count": 22,
      "author_id": "UClgmf_qbRg_-RqYNtbJDVUg",
      "author": "@beorn9house",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m3FKI3KLREpcek6V16-dHtIOmMzv8BInlcwiTxKrfAZU8=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxATdB3JdwrNe",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAQ-ogsyyb1D",
      "text": " @beorn9house  Completely agree with @nitroyetvn that it’s a mistake to romanticize emotions as something “special and separate” from thinking; that really does smell like old-fashioned dualism.\nBut the very fact that evolution developed complex emotional systems in the human brain is the most direct evidence that consciousness is not a monolith or a pure logical processor: it emerges from the hierarchical integration of multiple levels of mostly non-conscious subsystems (subcortical homeostasis, limbic valence, reward prediction).\nThese “primitive” subsystems generate the value signals that the vmPFC and executive cortex then integrate and broadcast globally. Without them — as in the classic Damasio/Elliot case that Ilya mentioned (taking hours to choose socks) — even “logic” itself fails to function.\nIt’s not that emotions are some magical source of value; they are the biological infrastructure that makes value possible in the first place, and therefore consciousness and decision-making. All integrated circuits, zero dualism. Great thread!",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCoOML76vmPMXeEvWSmSJDnw",
      "author": "@ialman2",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kLsmFv-bwUtfOoW5jVvl1aFt_CUw2fncnK1qS8O4DEa_bg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "1 month ago",

      "is_pinned": false

      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "Surely the connection between learning and emotions (e.g. trying to predict/maximize emotional rewards) could be described exactly as \"integrating emotions and logic\"? It doesn't seem that Ilya was trying to be very precise with his language here.",

    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAQ-49EfQCNd",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPyFgs8ONPi",
      "text": "​ @Videolistener  Yeah I think it's a mistake many people make to valorize emotions as something special and separate from thinking or decision making. The idea that a smart automaton with no emotions or a hive of ultra intelligent soulless creatures is interesting science fiction, but not based in biology at all. The idea that emotion are some special separate thing also rhymes a lot with long-bunked mind-body duality ways of thinking.\n\nEmotions evolved for the same reason as everything else: adapting to environment, aiding survival. They are just a more coarse-grained form of prediction and decision making, nothing categorically separate. When a worm with 320 neurons has a negative response to some smell in the environment, causing a chemical cascade through its body and ultimately goes left instead of right, this is the early precursor in evolutionary terms to all modern emotions.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCp7lo1FG1uyO-y6WjnjI0yA",
      "author": "@nitroyetevn",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mDarYKA7CVOKDMfzxgWokHNd5gI6sxn1FU9RYf8Q=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAQ-EMv-p8QO",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPyFgs8ONPi",
      "text": " @Videolistener  Emotions are an earlier evolutionary mechanism, giving rise to fight or flight, etc adaptive responses. A clear perceptual signal triggers release of brain chemicals causing the brain to operate in a different adaptive way to the the situation. Cognition is newer, and may well be leveraging emotions as the \"value function\" to determine whether a course of action is good or bad. The brain is predictive in nature, but what precisely is it predicting? Just action outcomes and sensory inputs perhaps, or maybe we're predicting emotional responses, and this is what drives action.",

      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "I was always fascinated by neuroscience and connectomics as a source of inspiration or even datasets to govern information systems. The challenge is that the exercise of directly transposing one to another is huge, because in the process you need to speak at least 4 languages - the brain, the brain representation, data science, and your own language. That's 3 translations, 1 data collection, and 1 communication, not to mention that each jump isn't just translational but research in its own right.\nTo your point, though, I feel that is even more insightful - the source of emotion remains, which means a value function and assignment exists, but the integrator mechanism is broken. It seems then like to take inspiration from this, what enables decisionmaking is the closed loop of emotion assignment and integrated action. Live learning and calibration is the source.",

      "author": "@Polymurple",

      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "I had the same reaction too.  I do remember watching a documentary Showing a patient  Whose brain was damaged on the part of the function responsible for making decisions,as a result,he was not able to make simple decisions like buying Which yoga at the grocery store.",
      "like_count": 0,

      "author": "@haiyan3478",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_krZTe_tp7hhkcljTnLp4kQ1MtHsh136qKLxFUk6yJo75ZC=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAR--LOYUr5t",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "Considering that biology hasn't solved what a brain actually is and does to the degree that we could put it into algorithms, I'm not sure that AI researchers trying to understand the bits we do know is the only potential solution. \n\nUnderstanding what intelligence actually is probably doesn't need study of the human brain at all ...",

      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "Agreed, but don’t you think ai developers should be focusing more on brain lesion studies? For the last few years there seems to have been little interest in this.",

    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPy6Hpb9xCt",

      "text": "​ @ScrollingSerf Yes, definitely. But to do that top researchers like Ilya needs to study a minimum om neuropsychiatric research I think.",
      "like_count": 38,

    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAQ0nhClPOR_",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPy6Hpb9xCt",
      "text": "​ @HenrikSahlinPettersen  given the mix-up is on your part (not Ilya's) and you're risking to mislead a  lot of people, I think it would show good form to correct yourself",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UC-3QQDijyAFi8FgMoL05MyQ",
      "author": "@sfz82",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_khaYSe6iLmMW-uQkeUtLXRrYHUIJquJ8xI2oyoAME=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,

      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,

    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAQ2HkeRxrWU",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPy6Hpb9xCt",
      "text": "I don't believe a correction is warranted; the distinction is central to the architectural lesson for AI. The mix-up is conflating the vmPFC (high-level neocortical integrator) with the 'emotional center' (primitive limbic system).\n​The patient Ilya mentions had damage to the vmPFC. Under the Somatic Marker Hypothesis, this causes a failure of 'Secondary Induction' which is the ability to trigger value signals from thoughts and plans. If we tell AI researchers that the 'value function' is just the primitive emotional brain, they might build the wrong architecture. We need the bridge (vmPFC), not just the engine.",
      "like_count": 9,
      "author_id": "UC51GMeWn8P4pBUQmZCP0MWw",
      "author": "@HenrikSahlinPettersen",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n66UAKQjmBhvaye6fkZCpqK__AfRuojpApjH7KAK9oryo=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPyJhDm_sSJ",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "Quote from Damasios \"Descartes Error\":\n\"First, there is a region of the human brain, the ventromedial prefrontal cortices, whose damage consistently compromises, in as pure a fashion as one is likely to find, both reasoning/decision making, and emotion/feeling, especially in the personal and social domain.\"",
      "like_count": 10,
      "author_id": "UCa2TCoAf2bTjw1CVNaIcrqw",
      "author": "@bilderzucht",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/QE3xuvEShV5D4vnii8p01wF_aaW0Q3DnFBeAlMf9e7jM89Ne4r3Oq1Y2vFkPXJACnHez6Tpy-g=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAQ2MEHt4vW-",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPyJhDm_sSJ",
      "text": "​​ @bilderzucht Yes, exactly. It's the integrator of the primitive emotional and neocortical brain, not the emotional brain itself. It's more complex than that, hence the comment that damage to the emotional brain results primarily in executive dysfunction is misleading and a potentially dangerous oversimplification.",
      "like_count": 5,
      "author_id": "UC51GMeWn8P4pBUQmZCP0MWw",
      "author": "@HenrikSahlinPettersen",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n66UAKQjmBhvaye6fkZCpqK__AfRuojpApjH7KAK9oryo=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPyGlNdtOWD",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "Huh? Ilya is spot on. Amygdala lesions affect decision making just as VMPC lesions do. Check out Bechara's classic 1999 JNeuro paper with the Damasios, or Gupta et al., 2012 Neuropsychologia for a review",
      "like_count": 9,
      "author_id": "UC-3QQDijyAFi8FgMoL05MyQ",
      "author": "@sfz82",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_khaYSe6iLmMW-uQkeUtLXRrYHUIJquJ8xI2oyoAME=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAQ2ICBgaYDf",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPyGlNdtOWD",
      "text": "I appreciate the reference to Bechara (1999), but that paper actually reinforces my distinction. Bechara and Damasio explicitly distinguish between 'Primary Inducers' (mediated by the Amygdala) and 'Secondary Inducers' (mediated by the vmPFC).\n​The 'socks' example, characterized by getting stuck in an infinite logical loop, is a classic failure of Secondary Induction. This is the inability to trigger a somatic marker from a thought or simulation. While Amygdala damage does affect decision-making (specifically conditioning to immediate stimuli), the specific 'paralysis by analysis' regarding trivial logic is the hallmark of vmPFC damage (Damasio’s patient 'Elliot'). My point remains: for AI, we don't just need a 'feeling module' (the limbic system); we need the specific architecture that integrates high-level planning with those signals (vmPFC).",
      "like_count": 22,
      "author_id": "UC51GMeWn8P4pBUQmZCP0MWw",
      "author": "@HenrikSahlinPettersen",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n66UAKQjmBhvaye6fkZCpqK__AfRuojpApjH7KAK9oryo=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPy6WbZ8Oxm",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "I think Ilya's point is not that emotions, per se, are the missing value function (that AIs are missing now) but that there is something in the structure of the brain that evolution gave us beyond the neural structure that we rely on for our intelligence.  He was coy about saying what exactly that is, but he wants to do research to find out.",
      "like_count": 28,
      "author_id": "UCBubHpuvgSHTYbSxISQNrhA",
      "author": "@zeeraViewer",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kZ1JOx1dohLbwLHF7FF3_oDyP0oMNO-6F2urJCLgs=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPy7S-RreAi",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPy6WbZ8Oxm",
      "text": "​ @zeeraViewer Yes, definitely agree and I understand what he's getting at with emotions being the value function. However, when you give an example from well known brain lesion litterature it would be good to get it right, otherwise the \"simplistic analogy\" sort of falls short, when referring to a cortical structure rather than a limbic \"old brain\" structure.",
      "like_count": 60,
      "author_id": "UC51GMeWn8P4pBUQmZCP0MWw",
      "author": "@HenrikSahlinPettersen",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n66UAKQjmBhvaye6fkZCpqK__AfRuojpApjH7KAK9oryo=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPzqeJPe5UZ",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPy7S-RreAi",
      "text": " @HenrikSahlinPettersen I think he was referring to amygdala damages. They end up impairing decision making. He’s right in that.\n\nBut there are other things to which he’s given very little thought. One is his belief that humans learn things fast with very little pre training. We’ve had 1 billion years of evolution to perfect our world modeling abilities. And I’m referring to how to take photons, air pressure and single atoms and transform them into colors, shapes, sounds and smells. All in a coherent way. That is the fundamental base of intelligence that AIs are lacking. Our evolutionary threads were exposed to amounts of data that make the whole internet pale in comparison.\nThis interview has not convinced me that he’s on the right path.",
      "like_count": 4,
      "author_id": "UCgiXIo4E7G4tGnVhWFGgTJQ",
      "author": "@matteoianni9372",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kOV-3Og8yPn5U4WhoI2_75t_kOQbOEY7Bzu3a-WruIow=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1766102400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAQ2Ixzlbbal",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPy7S-RreAi",
      "text": "​ @matteoianni9372 Good points. However, the specific example Ilya gave (taking hours to decide on socks) is the famous case of 'Elliot' from Damasio's Descartes' Error, who had damage to the vmPFC, not the Amygdala.\n​While Amygdala damage does impair decision-making, it typically leads to risky behavior (a failure of 'Primary Inducers'). The 'paralysis by analysis' Ilya described is distinctly a vmPFC failure (a failure of 'Secondary Inducers'). The patient gets stuck because they can’t trigger a value signal from a thought or future plan. This distinction is key for AI: we don't just need a primitive emotional center; we need the high-level architecture that integrates those values into our logic.",
      "like_count": 3,
      "author_id": "UC51GMeWn8P4pBUQmZCP0MWw",
      "author": "@HenrikSahlinPettersen",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n66UAKQjmBhvaye6fkZCpqK__AfRuojpApjH7KAK9oryo=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "this is an extremely useful distinction, that's for clearing it up. i'm a neuroscience phd student, and had a big \"huh?\" moment there, but wasn't familiar with the case and just kept listening. while his miss was quite bad, i reckon that the example of the vmPFC connects beautifully with his notion that it's important to take strong inspiration from the brain. as far as i'm aware, current AI models lack executive networks; i think that promoting formation of executive networks, either through explicit design or learning rules, could be a critical step toward building robust machine intelligence.",
      "like_count": 8,
      "author_id": "UC5CJLomyhQz79Ri0am_OcsA",
      "author": "@nthngh",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_k7QQB5V0EwAzk7QGxOZEDKT_2FZ22TT5kXfDEkOKEjZ1-nx0DyAEVAPxAMsVElIxxWFQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAQ194dIWZ6Q",

      "text": "​ @nthngh but the multi-layered NN architecture is available. Isn't that related to executive network?",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCtdMe2P4kp9aigJTzQebFGg",
      "author": "@chaz-e",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nJta_qUN2uXP0stsUUiBLrZb3wqa_pm1GmNqsqNJO7Wg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAQ-lfPJrTkS",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "The point of Damasio was that emotions are deeply baked in “the executive function” which used to be seen as fully rational",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCfNs4la3O9y5nLI4L_Y5EGw",
      "author": "@KoluCola",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_ldnRaMXo3Xbz4m16flfWdwc-2kFbIWdt-Bidg_Wmqk8lgn08iWiJ8zzWKtP_mN96n1pQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,

      "_time_text": "4 months ago",

    {
      "id": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg.APxymdOXuVxAPyz16CwxtN",
      "parent": "Ugyfma3Epou-lY1cQFh4AaABAg",
      "text": "Henrik. You're absolutely right to point out the anatomical distinction—the ventromedial prefrontal cortex is indeed an executive integration center rather than a primitive emotional structure, and that precision matters when drawing insights from neuroscience.\r\n\r\nThe vmPFC damage case reveals something profound: it's not just that emotions exist, but that high-level integration between affective signals and executive reasoning is essential for functional decision-making. The fact that disrupting this integration—rather than eliminating emotions themselves—causes the decision-making paralysis suggests that the architecture of this coupling may be as important as the components themselves.\r\n\r\nWhat we're really seeing is that decision-making requires a \"closed loop\" between value assignment and integrated action. The vmPFC lesion studies show us that having both systems intact but disconnected is insufficient—the integration mechanism itself is critical.\r\n\r\nThis actually reinforces the case for neuroscience-informed AI research, though as you and others note, it requires genuine engagement with the neuropsychiatric literature rather than simplified analogies. The challenge is navigating multiple domains of expertise simultaneously—but that interdisciplinary rigor is precisely what's needed to extract meaningful architectural insights from neuroscience.",
      "like_count": 6,
      "author_id": "UCodJDYDjmeln9B7QJghZK4A",
      "author": "@laviefu0630",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l5I8GNRHWA7t3aF1Sk9xIuRSyteLgqqUDiKePbcJ2Bi3FZ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
