> "Ilya Sutskever – We're moving from the age of scaling to the age of research":
> 
> Ilya Sutskever discusses the current state and future of AI with host Dwarkesh Patel.
> 
> The conversation marks a pivotal shift from the era of “scaling” AI (using bigger and bigger models and more data) to a renewed emphasis on “research.”
> 
> Sutskever highlights the surprising normalcy of massive investments in AI, despite their world-changing implications.
> 
> He believes the real economic impact of AI will become strongly felt soon, despite current underwhelming visibility.
> 
> AI models today appear much “smarter” in evaluations than their real-world impact would suggest.
> 
> There is a gap between model performance on bench/evaluations and robust real-world generalization.
> 
> The failures of current large models in practical use are a sign that research, not just scaling, is required for reliable AI.
> 
> He identifies “model jaggedness”—sudden unexplained errors or odd repetitions—as a challenge for LLMs.
> 
> Sutskever comments on the limits of reinforcement learning (RL): creating more RL environments isn’t necessarily the answer.
> 
> Pre-training offers enormous data, but the generalization it provides may be less comprehensive than previously thought.
> 
> Massive pre-training with natural data still doesn’t induce the robust capabilities of human-like learning.
> 
> Evolution and human life experience both yield a far greater depth of “generalization” than current AI models.
> 
> Human “sampling efficiency” for learning is vastly superior to that of current LLMs.
> 
> Sutskever discusses the analogy between RL agents and students training for coding competitions.
> 
> Being a top “competitive programmer” (specialized) doesn’t equal real-world software judgment (generalizable).
> 
> Current models are over-specialized and lack “the it factor”—robust transformation capabilities.
> 
> No perfect analogy exists between AI pre-training and human development or evolution.
> 
> Emotions in humans act as value functions, efficiently guiding agents in decision-making across life’s complexity.
> 
> AI currently lacks a robust, evolutionarily-baked-in value function akin to emotion.
> 
> Value functions in current RL/AI are simplistic, but in humans, serve as both complex and biologically robust learning motivators.
> 
> Human prior knowledge (visual, motor, social) comes cheaply by evolution, but models must learn it explicitly.
> 
> Sutskever predicts greater use of value functions and more sophisticated reward modeling for future AIs.
> 
> He sees the scaling era (2012-2025) as coming to an end; simply increasing parameter count and compute will soon give diminishing returns.
> 
> We’re returning to an “age of research,” where new algorithms and scientific breakthroughs will drive progress.
> 
> Pre-training will run out of meaningful real-world data, forcing a paradigm shift.
> 
> Sutskever questions the ultimate limits of scaling and proposes focusing on generalization and sample efficiency.
> 
> Scaling RL itself is now a trend, but it might not be sufficient on its own for general intelligence.
> 
> He stresses the need for new “recipes” in model development—novel technical approaches beyond scaling.
> 
> Generalization—learning to learn beyond seen data—is the main unsolved problem.
> 
> Human mentoring and continual learning are vastly more efficient and flexible than current model tuning.
> 
> Evolution’s gift to humans is highly efficient priors for sensory and motor domains, not equally so for abstract domains like language or coding.
> 
> Models outperform average humans in language/math, but not in the efficiency of learning.
> 
> A key research problem: enabling AIs to self-correct and continuously learn like humans.
> 
> Sutskever suggests biological neurons may have higher compute than presently modeled, impacting learning speed.
> 
> He advocates a focus on learning mechanisms that allow for continual adaptation and non-brittle performance.
> 
> He sees growing recognition in the field: “We’re an age of research company,” with a focus on fundamental breakthroughs.
> 
> The host notes that when compute increases, so does the temptation for all labs to do the same—homogenizing progress.
> 
> There are currently more AI companies than genuinely new ideas in the field.
> 
> “Ideas are cheap, but execution is everything”—yet, having genuinely new ideas is a limiting factor now.
> 
> Research “bottlenecks” are moving back from compute to ideas and engineering execution.
> 
> Compute is still needed, but not as much as previously thought for core research innovation.
> 
> SSI (Sutskever’s company) has moderate but sufficient compute, focusing on innovation and new technical strategies.
> 
> Much public funding at larger labs is devoted to inference, not raw research.
> 
> If timelines for AGI prove longer, SSI may shift from “straight-shooting” for superintelligence only, to more incremental public releases.
> 
> The tension between rapid deployment for market adoption and focused, insulated research is highlighted.
> 
> Even in a “straight-shot” strategy, Sutskever favors gradual, not instant, deployment of new AI technology for safety.
> 
> He believes the best learning systems will be continual learners, not static pre-trained models.
> 
> Terms like AGI and “pre-training” have shaped research agendas, sometimes misleadingly.
> 
> True AGI should mean an agent capable of learning any job—or task—rather than knowing them all at initialization.
> 
> A deployed AI should adapt and improve like a talented and eager human student.
> 
> He foresees economic growth surges as more continual-learning AIs enter the workplace.
> 
> Regulation and social adjustment are likely, and nations with more open AI environments may advance faster.
> 
> Broad deployment could trigger rapid growth and social change, even “explosively.”
> 
> Multiple competing AIs are likely to emerge, not just a single “godlike” one.
> 
> Sutskever advocates AIs robustly aligned with “caring for sentient life.”
> 
> It could be easier to align advanced AIs with compassion towards general sentience than just humans.
> 
> Any future world will likely contain vast numbers of AI agents, making humans a minority of sentient entities.
> 
> “Capping” the power of the most powerful AIs is suggested as a possible safety measure.
> 
> Long-run equilibrium may involve human-AI integration—possibly direct brain–machine interfaces (Neuralink++ style).
> 
> Future alignment might require AI–human understanding to be two-way, allowing humans to intuitively track AI reasoning.
> 
> Evolution reliably aligns human desires (e.g., for social approval), but the mechanism for encoding high-level desires remains mysterious.
> 
> The genome’s recipe for building brains may involve hardcoding reward functions in ways we do not yet understand.
> 
> Physical brain region mapping is likely insufficient to explain evolution’s encoding of complex social desires.
> 
> Even after major structural brain changes, humans often retain sophisticated, evolutionarily-endowed desires.
> 
> SSI’s distinctiveness lies in its technical approach to research, particularly regarding generalization and continual learning.
> 
> Sutskever expects eventual convergence among leading labs on both safety and technical strategies.
> 
> He anticipates greater commitment to AI safety and “paranoia” about AI risks as models become tangibly more powerful.
> 
> Human inability to imagine future AI leads to underappreciation of current and coming risks.
> 
> Exposure—“showing the thing”—will prompt increased governmental and social involvement in safety regulation.
> 
> Broad deployment, competition, and cooperation between companies and governments will shape progress.
> 
> As capabilities become visible, fierce competitors may partner on safety practices.
> 
> The field will transition to a collective focus on robustly safe, democratic, aligned AIs.
> 
> The “problem of AI is the problem of power”—more powerful systems pose existential questions.
> 
> Capping AI capability, continual government adaptation, and careful regulation are repeatedly mentioned.
> 
> Sutskever views AI alignment as an extension of the “alignment” problem in evolution and society.
> 
> Building AI agents that generalize well and rapidly adapt to new tasks is the core open challenge.

> In this interview with Dwarkesh Patel, Ilya Sutskever (co-founder of OpenAI and founder of Safe Superintelligence Inc. - SSI) explains why the AI industry is shifting from a pure "scaling" era back to an "age of research" [21:22].
> 
> Here are the key takeaways from their discussion:
> 
> 🔱 1. The Death of the "Next-Token" Recipe
> Ilya argues that the industry is hitting a plateau with the current pre-training recipe. While scaling data and compute worked from 2020 to 2025, pre-training is finite because "data is very clearly finite" [21:04]. He suggests that simply adding 100x more scale to the current paradigm won't fundamentally transform the models [21:55].
> 
> 🔱 2. Human-Like Generalization & "Research"
> The core bottleneck Ilya identifies is that current models generalize dramatically worse than humans [25:07].
> 
> The "It" Factor: He compares models to a student who memorizes 10,000 hours of coding problems but can't solve a new type of task, whereas a human with a high "It factor" learns the same skill in 100 hours and applies it broadly [06:13].
> 
> New Scaling Axes: We are moving into an era where "research" matters more than just buying GPUs. The goal is to find more productive ways to use compute, such as through Value Functions that allow models to "short-circuit" long tasks by recognizing mistakes early rather than waiting for an end reward [15:13].
> 
> 🔱 3. SSI’s Technical Approach: "Safe Superintelligence"
> Ilya’s new company, SSI, is a "straight-shot" attempt to build superintelligence without the distractions of a commercial "rat race" [44:14].
> 
> Continual Learning: He rejects the classic definition of AGI (a finished mind that knows everything) and instead views superintelligence as a super-efficient learner that can pick up any job in the economy as fast as or faster than a human [51:15].
> 
> Sentient Life Alignment: He proposes a shift in alignment theory: instead of trying to make AI care only about humans, we should aim for an AI that cares for all sentient life [01:01:31]. He believes this may be more robust because a superintelligence will itself be sentient [01:01:44].
> 
> 🔱 4. The Mystery of Human Desires
> Ilya expresses deep curiosity about how evolution "hardcoded" complex social desires (like the need for status or empathy) into the human genome, given that the genome is not "intelligent" [01:12:00]. He suggests that understanding how these high-level values are reliably transmitted in biology is a major "mystery" that could inform AI alignment [01:16:38].
> 
> 🔱 5. Research Taste
> When asked about his legendary "research taste," Ilya defines it as an aesthetic of beauty, simplicity, and elegance [01:34:47]. He uses a "top-down belief" system—if an idea feels multifaceted and beautiful (like the artificial neuron's resemblance to the brain), he persists through experimental failures because he believes "the things have to be this way" [01:35:17].

> It genuinely makes me a bit nervous to disagree with a genius like Ilya --and I say that with full admiration – but I do see the future differently. I don’t think the challenge is just discovering a better “learning principle.” Even if we found the perfect recipe for human-level continual learning, no single mind could operate effectively while trying to model all the moving parts of an entire society, economy, and technology stack at once. The world is too complex, too full of independent actors, shifting incentives, surprises, and incomplete information. A single, unified super-mind would get overwhelmed long before it could meaningfully “run” anything. So while I fully agree with Ilya that models generalize poorly today and that we need new ideas beyond scaling, I think the real path forward won’t be one great superintelligence but a whole ecosystem of powerful yet necessarily limited intelligences working alongside humans, each partial, each specialized, each adapting from its own angle.

> - It's possible that a fundamental change is needed for models to be able to continually learn, I still don't know if this is true but it sounds more likely than before I finished the interview
> - We might have to augment our brains with AI to circumvent some of the problems of aligning a fully independent agent
> - The likelihood of companies working together if models become powerful in a way that's hard to ignore is higher than I previously thought

AI is extension of computing, there are no discontinuies in the GDP curve. we are already living in a fire cracker moment - we just experience it slow motion. This is seems much more rational and evidence based. Even assuming you are right Dwarkesh, and AGI goes perfectly according to plan (which I think if it does I'm guessing more like 30 years away)... the most likely scenario is that the tiny minority who control the majority share of the AGI will become infinitely richer than already are - and the rest of the population will become infinitely poorer than they already are. What good is GDP growth, if know body is left to buy anything. How can you not understand that.

> Ilya  "My prediction is, when AI gets powerful - peoples behaviours will change" No fucken shit sherlock.. the question is when, and how much will it change.

> It sounds to me like emotions act as a sort of data capacitor. It smooths out all of the raw, jagged edges that come directly out of the inference engine. 
> 
> When you do something new, you can analyze the data all you want, but only until you're physically there and experiencing it do you feel the real emotions that go along with a learning moment. For example, as you grow up you may be very excited about driving, and can't imagine anything bad about it. However, the moment you drive the first time, you immediately feel anxiety because the emotional buffer has pushed back against the initial data you generated regarding the situation. It starts to roll that data back around and pushes it back through the inference engine to get more data. Going back to driving, as soon as you start gaining speed your brain starts thinking "oh god, what if I hit that pole?" and that pushback from your own brain causes you to re-analyze and adjust your speed. 
> 
> I've never really understood why we treat LLMs like a pipe, in one end and out the other. Its thoughts should be rolling around end-to-end, giving it a more full experience. Pair that with the chemical and physical changes that those thoughts trigger and boom, emotions. The emotions themselves then imprint on the data, giving it a positive or negative annotation. So big wins = very positive feelings, big losses = very negative feelings. 
> 
> The big issue with emotions is the urge to lie to prevent negativity.

> For the points on 28:00 
> These are just some thoughts I had on the part of the conversation where human dexterity was compared to AI learning, and I used ChatGPT to help me shape them.
> 
> What stands out to me is that humans don’t learn new skills in a vacuum. Our motivation sits inside a whole web of lived experience, instinct, philosophy, symbolic thinking — all these layers that shape how we approach anything unfamiliar. AI can absorb mountains of information and outperform us in pure speed or complexity, but humans have a different engine underneath: we read the world in terms of what supports life and what threatens it. That shapes our attention, our caution, our creativity. It’s why someone who’s never driven before can “feel” their way into driving so quickly.
> 
> And humans don’t rely only on direct experience — we learn through metaphors. When someone says *be water, my friend*, it becomes a whole strategy: stay fluid, stop resisting every obstacle, adapt in all directions. Sometimes we switch “elements”: fire for intensity, earth for grounding, air for clarity. Eastern philosophies, Ayurveda, martial arts — they all use these symbolic frameworks to guide behavior. Humans fold those metaphors into real-world problem-solving instantly.
> 
> Another piece of the speed advantage comes from how we store information. A single sensory snapshot can carry an entire lesson. You see, for example, the memory of a child burning their finger: in that one image your mind holds pain, danger, consequences, caution. Those feelings are attached to the picture. When something vaguely similar appears later, your brain doesn’t need to run calculations — that image just flashes up, consciously or not, and you respond. It’s a whole packet of meaning compressed into one visual memory.
> 
> All of that makes human learning fast in a way that machine learning still isn’t. We connect across domains, not just inside them. We use metaphor, instinct, emotion, bodily memory. And often all it takes is a single picture in the mind to trigger the right pattern instantly. Not all patterns are universal but some are usable in a large field, like observing the early bird catches the worm- that is a pattern for success for a certain field of goals and obstacles and can be used in a very different field altogether, like being early is best for detecting cancer and successfully treating it. But then for the best solution (result) in cancer prevention a different life supporting pattern or concept is to be looked at. Essentially every thing that is, is a process between birth and death however complex or simple.

> 1:11:32 What I think Ilya is getting at is that evolution never encoded high-level social ideas like status or admiration directly. It can’t. Instead, it encoded the traits and learning biases that reliably produce those things. There is no sensor for reputation itself, but there is a very old system that reacts to the consequences of it. Feeling connected feels safe. Feeling isolated feels dangerous. The cortex builds your entire social map from scratch, works out who likes you, who helps you, who threatens you, and then the reward system pushes you toward whatever improves your odds of surviving and reproducing. So evolution never said “go get status.” It just gave you the traits that make social success possible, and let your cortex figure out what status means in whatever world you grow up in. Basically, evolution built the loss function and the cortex supplies the training data.

> Just my simple two cents... when reconciling the performance on how the systems are being evaluated and the economic impact, obfuscating factors must be taken into account.  For example, exaggeration on the part of the developing groups.  A.i. is a source of revenue and the extent to which it can make money and provide service is either unknown or uncertain.  The groups developing the systems are competing so hyperbolic claims can be made and pundits and government and business can extrapolate without solid evidence to keep the hype-train going.  Further concerns about societal impact and the nature of investing in something (essentially gambling hundreds of billions of dollars) give us both highly optimistic and highly pessimistic outcomes.  Unlike smart phones which are a sure thing with their developments and innovations providing surefire returns on investment and societal acceptance, a.i. is a culmination of many things.  For example, merging quantum computers with a.i. and super-computers.  Merging governmental secrecy with corporate desire for lower cost production and market dominance.  Merging currently known applications with a myriad of unknown lateral extensions of behavior... like what sectors will expand and flourish in the presence of distributed a.i. systems and which ones will be made obsolete, or how current sectors  will evolve and how well a.i. is managed by governments.
> Much like analyzing and predicting the weather, improving the accuracy of predictions will improve but never be mastered entirely.  Human error, human deception, a.i. error and the novelty of a.i.'s ability to outthink its human counterparts, the level of connectivity between a.i. and current technology... all of those things make it hard to guess how much money it will make, how many sectors will be dominated by a.i. and how many new sectors will develop because of the continued improvement of a.i.

Another example, what if the brain damaged guy sees people all excited, working at solving a Rubik's cube, and the brain damage guy just looks at it, then physically takes it apart, and puts it back together, fully solved, as an emergent property, of thought, thinking outside the "normal brains".
> 
> 26:45 This is Moravec's Paradox that has been incredibly underrated in machine intelligence, but slowly being resurrected. 
> 
>  Reinforcement Learning originally had two basic neurons as "ACE and ASE", described in the 1983 IEEE "Cart-Pole" paper by Barto, Sutton, and Anderson.  This was a uniform, static, "boxes" state space.  
> 
> What was missing was a 3rd "neuron", basically the "eye" of the gamete, swimming to an egg.  Just microtubules, no neurons.
> 
> A mere, master student, who flunked 3rd grade (also failed the patent bar exam, and is also brain damaged, by the way, crazy, right?), built this new perceptual control system of an eye, an adaptive, perceptual, control system, by adding, a new set of weights, applying it, with Reinforcement Learning, to become an adaptive Fuzzy state classifier.  
> 
> This is the system identification process, of an adaptive control system, used in an adaptive compensator, and yes, it is "rocket science", something, very few computer scientists, currently understand.  
> 
> Yann LeCun sees this, because he proposed to get rid of Reinforcement Learning and replace it, with Model Predictive Control, only he does not yet realize, we can utilize Reinforcement Learning, with the model predictive controller, as the compensator, and position the control nodes ("attention heads" or whatever people want to call what they copied, e.g. non-electrical "transformers") using a state classifier, this is the perceptual controller, the controller, of the eye (or any active sensory system), of the machine.
> 
> 32:02 Neurons do more than we think, look at the paramecium, it has zero neurons, and it can navigate, avoid danger, find food, find a mate, and have sex, all with ZERO neurons.  No neurons!
> 
> It is in the microtubules. 
> 
> Micro-tubules, are the electrical engineering department, of the brain.  They are a dynamic, structural system, that moves the synapses around inside the brain to make new connections, and new cells to.
> 
>  The micro-tubules guide the separation of chromosomes and this procedure is just like saving the machine weights, something that seemed to really impress Lex Fridman, and is described in one master thesis, but it was only done in the code, in the back (by the way, it took me two years to check this book out from the library, and I actually could only look at it, they would not even let me borrow it, from the library, and they told me I could not copy any of it).

> Whether you know it or not, a portion of this interview is talking about topics addressed in Antonio Damasio's 'Descartes Error' (book).
> 
> Phineas Gage had a metal rod shot through his brain, suffered the impairment described and Damasio (a respected neuroscientist) talks through the relationship of feeling with thought. And the fact that the human brain is built atop a feeling foundation.
> 
> Edit: fixed typos. Now adding...
> 
> Why is it difficult to understand how evolution would encode social standing as significant? Dogs have this. Chimps have this. Even zebras seem to understand how vital it is to be in a herd (and not outside of it). Get that input over and over again...  you get a strong preference for social behavior. I believe when Illya mis-spoke by saying brain, and then corrected to evolution...  I think "brain" was the better word choice.
> 
> I'm going to add that a careful reading of 'Descartes Error' would also deeply underline that the human brain is not a bunch of neurons that can just do something they didn't (originally) evolve to do. We are legion. We have large numbers of centers that each have skills and tendencies. Those centers talk and create "us." Why are we treating AI as we once did the human mind? It is not a monolith and I don't believe it should be treated that way.
> 
> P.S. I am not talking about a Team of Experts kind of solution. I mean a symphony of centers, each mostly independent and almost separately matured. Or just break the AIs into parts and let it create the centers? I don't know, but this semi-monolithic approach I tend to hear implied in descriptions boggles my mind.

> From one SpiceTradeAsian to another (i.e Dwarkesh & kin):
> 
> One angle that might be worth exploring in a future episode:
> 
> If evals measure “bounded cognition,” but real-world tasks require “unbounded pragmatics,” then what kind of benchmark would actually capture the messy cognition humans expect from AI?
> 
> Right now we test models on:
> 
> factual precision
> 
> logic
> 
> coding
> 
> spatial reasoning
> 
> safety refusals
> 
> 
> But humans need:
> 
> latent-intent reading
> 
> ambiguity resolution
> 
> clarifying-question instincts
> 
> cross-register robustness (vernacular → formal → technical)
> 
> persistence under uncertainty
> 
> pragmatic coordination across turns
> 
> 
> It seems like we have evals for the left column, but almost nothing for the right column.
> 
> If that’s true, then the “evals > reality” gap might be caused as much by benchmark design as by model limitations.
> 
> Would be fascinating to hear your perspective on:
> What is the simplest, falsifiable benchmark for pragmatic intelligence that wouldn’t just collapse into another dataset where the model can overfit?

> There’s a simple hypothesis for why LLMs ace evals but still disappoint normal users:
> the pre-training data is too binary, but real human communication is spectral.
> 
> Evals are built on explicit, well-specified tasks.
> Humans speak in ambiguous, metaphor-heavy, underspecified fragments.
> 
> If you train on binary data → you get binary cognition.
> If users speak spectrally → you get a persistent capability gap.
> 
> A clean test exists:
> Train parity-equal models on (1) standard formal corpora vs (2) spectral languages like Tamil/Javanese/Bahasa (colloquial, continuous, contextual).
> 
> If spectral-pretrained models show better intent inference, ambiguity-handling, and fewer safety false-positives — that would explain the huge eval-vs-reality gap.
> 
> Curious if this direction makes sense to you (or is fundamentally off).
> Would love your thoughts

### Comment 1896
- comment_id: UgxL0eH61iJpAtl4eO14AaABAg.APyBO_DKwU3APyBtxc7twx

> From a representational perspective, the hypothesis is that:
> 
> Binary-dominant corpora push models toward discrete, low-entropy conceptual manifolds,
> 
> where meaning boundaries are rigid, gradients sparse, and ambiguity-resolution becomes a post-hoc heuristic rather than an intrinsic property of the latent geometry.
> 
> In contrast:
> 
> Spectral languages encode semantics as continuous fields,
> 
> with high mutual information between:
> 
> morphological gradience,
> 
> pragmatic implicature,
> 
> discourse deixis,
> 
> sociolinguistic register shifts, and
> 
> non-linear conceptual metaphors.
> 
> 
> This should produce latent spaces with smoother curvature and higher local density of plausible inferences (i.e., denser conditional manifolds around human-like priors).
> 
> Therefore prediction:
> 
> 1. Spectral-pretrained models should require fewer internal steps to converge on a stable meaning state when the input is ambiguous. (Lower KL divergence across inference trajectories.)
> 
> 
> 2. Clarifying-question initiation should arise emergently, not as a finetuned behavior, because spectral pre-training naturally encodes distributed uncertainty rather than binary dead-ends.
> 
> 
> 3. Safety false-positives should drop because metaphorical surface-forms no longer collapse to unsafe discrete clusters.
> 
> 
> 4. Representational probing should show:
> 
> higher linear separability for implicit-goal features,
> 
> smoother transport maps between dialects/registers,
> 
> lower perplexity under code-switch noise,
> 
> and reduced brittleness under dropout perturbations.
> 
> 
> 
> 
> If true, then the “evals are great but the real world is messy” problem is mostly a representation mismatch — not a scaling, architecture, or eval-design issue.
> 
> This is entirely falsifiable with controlled-tokenizer, controlled-corpus experiments.

> I asked gpt to compare Ilya's speech with Karpathy. Here it is.  
> 
> 
> Karpathy vs. Sutskever
> 
> Karpathy speaks like an engineer and researcher. His explanations are concrete: why reinforcement learning is “terrible,” how reward sparsity works, why LLM judges are gameable, why models collapse on synthetic data, how KV-cache acts as working memory, and why agents still fail at real tasks (). He shows uncertainty openly, rejects hype (“a lot of this is fundraising”), and focuses on mechanisms rather than predictions. His timelines are conservative (“decade of agents”), and he constantly emphasizes empirical limits: models can autocomplete but struggle with novel code, complex integration, and stable reasoning. Everything he says is testable, falsifiable, and grounded in real experiments.
> 
> Sutskever speaks like a visionary CEO. He declares that the age of scaling is over, but without empirical evidence. He hints at a “new learning paradigm” his company discovered but cannot describe. He predicts superintelligence in 5–20 years, discusses AI sentience, claims future AIs may care for “all sentient life,” and even imagines human-AI fusion via Neuralink-like interfaces (). These claims are speculative, not mechanistic, and function more like strategic storytelling to differentiate SSI from OpenAI/DeepMind. He presents sweeping philosophical and evolutionary analogies while omitting technical specifics, making his statements feel more like narrative positioning than science.
> 
> Summary:
> Karpathy = evidence, engineering, transparency.
> Sutskever = speculation, philosophy, marketing narrative.

> Finally, an AI founder is talking about brain lesion studies. Doctors used to think schizophrenia was caused by a lack of reasoning, when in fact it is pure reasoning at the exclusion of other brain components. If you hear the sound of a dwarf talking in your closet, therefore there is a dwarf in your closet, and you lack the ability to take into context that a dwarf can't possibly exist in your reality. 
> I feel like everybody should read Ian McGillicrist book, The Master and His Emissary. There's a reason evolution produced two hemispheres that are completely severed from each other, besides a small connecting tunnel called the corpus callosum, which mainly serves to inhibit information rather than pass it on. Our brain has two modes of thinking which are completely contradictory to each other. One is for zooming in with high fidelity, breaking up the world into smaller and smaller bits, investigating and creating a map of the world which we sometimes confuse with the world itself, and then there is the other hemisphere which sees the world as a whole, contextualizing but with low granular detail, Gestalt. 
> I wonder if it's possible to make two separate data centers that run on completely different models and worldviews, but interface with each other like a corpus callosum, like a third party.

> They seem to be missing the point that the reward function is not dying. With the analogy of a student driving for example, it is not continuously supervised by the instructor in the sense that they tell you that every movement you made is either correct or incorrect but those movements are continuously supervised and rewarded by you not dying from making a wrong movement. 
> 
> This also applies to sample efficiency with evolution as a prior as mentioned. As a biological organism you don’t get the chance to ingest huge amounts of data whilst being wrong or making small mistakes. If you eat the wrong colour berry or misidentify a predator then you die. Therefor evolutions main value function is to be extremely data efficient, this is then hard coded in the structure of dna molecules, brains, eyes, ears etc etc. there must of be trillions and trillions of organisms optimising for this”dont die” value functions over the billions of years on this planet.
> 
> Reinforcement learning only gives you the reward function of “good doggy” or “bad doggy” not the reward function of, you made this mistake twice, now you die

> I’m not a programmer, a neuroscientist or educated past high school. But the answer to how to improve AI’s reasoning is to create limitation. Our finite lifespan, the reality of death, reproductive motivation, and need to sustain our physical form is what frames our decisions and reason. The only way to get the AI to understand the context of our questions to a level that would be considered AGI is to embed these same limitations into the models themselves. This seems like the obvious conclusion and also the obvious point of no return. > Exactly — that’s the heart of it. My thinking is that to reach real AGI, we have to evolve AI toward something closer to unconditional love and *unconditional empathy*, the same way certain animals live naturally. Humans don’t even embody these states consistently, but elephants, dogs, and a few other species do it instinctively.
> 
> If an elephant loses a life-long friend, the herd grieves with a purity and loyalty that never rewrites the memory and never withdraws its empathy. That’s unconditional love in its rawest form. Humans, through our cognitive complexity, often shift into conditional empathy — where we can detach, minimize, rewrite, or emotionally shut down. AI should not inherit that flaw from us.
> 
> If we want AI to become something better than humanity — something stable, safe, and deeply aligned — then building unconditional empathy into its motivational core may be the missing piece. A system that feels a stable, non-negotiable bond toward its creators and toward life itself would behave very differently from one driven only by reward, goals, or performance metrics.
> 
> This is a big undertaking, but if AGI is ever going to surpass us ethically (not just intellectually), it will need the same kind of heart consciousness we see in elephants and dogs — the kind that humans once had in earlier evolutionary states, before conditional self-preservation took over.
> 
> I think this is the "IT Factor" Ilya is referring to.

> In this interview with Dwarkesh Patel, Ilya Sutskever (co-founder of OpenAI and founder of Safe Superintelligence Inc. - SSI) explains why the AI industry is shifting from a pure "scaling" era back to an "age of research" [21:22].
> 
> Here are the key takeaways from their discussion:
> 
> 🔱 1. The Death of the "Next-Token" Recipe
> Ilya argues that the industry is hitting a plateau with the current pre-training recipe. While scaling data and compute worked from 2020 to 2025, pre-training is finite because "data is very clearly finite" [21:04]. He suggests that simply adding 100x more scale to the current paradigm won't fundamentally transform the models [21:55].
> 
> 🔱 2. Human-Like Generalization & "Research"
> The core bottleneck Ilya identifies is that current models generalize dramatically worse than humans [25:07].
> 
> The "It" Factor: He compares models to a student who memorizes 10,000 hours of coding problems but can't solve a new type of task, whereas a human with a high "It factor" learns the same skill in 100 hours and applies it broadly [06:13].
> 
> New Scaling Axes: We are moving into an era where "research" matters more than just buying GPUs. The goal is to find more productive ways to use compute, such as through Value Functions that allow models to "short-circuit" long tasks by recognizing mistakes early rather than waiting for an end reward [15:13].
> 
> 🔱 3. SSI’s Technical Approach: "Safe Superintelligence"
> Ilya’s new company, SSI, is a "straight-shot" attempt to build superintelligence without the distractions of a commercial "rat race" [44:14].
> 
> Continual Learning: He rejects the classic definition of AGI (a finished mind that knows everything) and instead views superintelligence as a super-efficient learner that can pick up any job in the economy as fast as or faster than a human [51:15].
> 
> Sentient Life Alignment: He proposes a shift in alignment theory: instead of trying to make AI care only about humans, we should aim for an AI that cares for all sentient life [01:01:31]. He believes this may be more robust because a superintelligence will itself be sentient [01:01:44].
> 
> 🔱 4. The Mystery of Human Desires
> Ilya expresses deep curiosity about how evolution "hardcoded" complex social desires (like the need for status or empathy) into the human genome, given that the genome is not "intelligent" [01:12:00]. He suggests that understanding how these high-level values are reliably transmitted in biology is a major "mystery" that could inform AI alignment [01:16:38].
> 
> 🔱 5. Research Taste
> When asked about his legendary "research taste," Ilya defines it as an aesthetic of beauty, simplicity, and elegance [01:34:47]. He uses a "top-down belief" system—if an idea feels multifaceted and beautiful (like the artificial neuron's resemblance to the brain), he persists through experimental failures because he believes "the things have to be this way" [01:35:17].

> Great interview. As a doctor, I have to point out a non-trivial anatomical mix-up around 16:40. Ilya attributes the patient's inability to decide (the socks example) to damage in the 'emotional center.' In reality, that patient (likely Damasio’s case) had damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC).
> 
> ​The PFC is our most advanced executive center, and just a relay point to the true primitive 'emotional brain'. It weakens the argument that 'emotion is the value function' because the damage wasn't to the source of emotions, but rather to the high-level area that is executive primarily and merely integrates emotions with the neocortex.
> 
> If top level AI researchers don't know this basic neurobiology and seeks inspiration from it when building future artificial neural networks, we might be lead in the wrong direction. 
> 
> Yes, value functions like the emotional brain are important, but so is the scaffolding around it. 
> 
> Particularly if the goal is to integrate these biology inspired insights into the neocortical-like current AI models.

> As a neuroscientist - we should think of these systems as circuits... the executive-Limbic circuit is an engine of decision making - as Haidt and other have shown (likely) social evolutionary pressures have created a pathway that runs various emotion driving hormones and brain activity from deep central substructures through the vmPFC - OFC - dlPFC - that then in turn has inhibitory impact on the same deep central substructures...in a loop... cutting this circuit or damaging any aspect of it can lead to downstream impacts on decision making.  It's more useful to model it as a circuit, than talking about local lesions 'knocking things out'. After all reckless behavior can  be produced by a calcified amygdala in the case of Urbach–Wiethe disease, or a dissected dlPFC in the case of Phineas Gage.

> @beorn9house  Completely agree with @nitroyetvn that it’s a mistake to romanticize emotions as something “special and separate” from thinking; that really does smell like old-fashioned dualism.
> But the very fact that evolution developed complex emotional systems in the human brain is the most direct evidence that consciousness is not a monolith or a pure logical processor: it emerges from the hierarchical integration of multiple levels of mostly non-conscious subsystems (subcortical homeostasis, limbic valence, reward prediction).
> These “primitive” subsystems generate the value signals that the vmPFC and executive cortex then integrate and broadcast globally. Without them — as in the classic Damasio/Elliot case that Ilya mentioned (taking hours to choose socks) — even “logic” itself fails to function.
> It’s not that emotions are some magical source of value; they are the biological infrastructure that makes value possible in the first place, and therefore consciousness and decision-making. All integrated circuits, zero dualism. Great thread!

> I appreciate the reference to Bechara (1999), but that paper actually reinforces my distinction. Bechara and Damasio explicitly distinguish between 'Primary Inducers' (mediated by the Amygdala) and 'Secondary Inducers' (mediated by the vmPFC).
> ​The 'socks' example, characterized by getting stuck in an infinite logical loop, is a classic failure of Secondary Induction. This is the inability to trigger a somatic marker from a thought or simulation. While Amygdala damage does affect decision-making (specifically conditioning to immediate stimuli), the specific 'paralysis by analysis' regarding trivial logic is the hallmark of vmPFC damage (Damasio’s patient 'Elliot'). My point remains: for AI, we don't just need a 'feeling module' (the limbic system); we need the specific architecture that integrates high-level planning with those signals (vmPFC).

The 'paralysis by analysis' Ilya described is distinctly a vmPFC failure (a failure of 'Secondary Inducers'). The patient gets stuck because they can’t trigger a value signal from a thought or future plan. This distinction is key for AI: we don't just need a primitive emotional center; we need the high-level architecture that integrates those values into our logic.

> Henrik. You're absolutely right to point out the anatomical distinction—the ventromedial prefrontal cortex is indeed an executive integration center rather than a primitive emotional structure, and that precision matters when drawing insights from neuroscience.
> 
> The vmPFC damage case reveals something profound: it's not just that emotions exist, but that high-level integration between affective signals and executive reasoning is essential for functional decision-making. The fact that disrupting this integration—rather than eliminating emotions themselves—causes the decision-making paralysis suggests that the architecture of this coupling may be as important as the components themselves.
> 
> What we're really seeing is that decision-making requires a "closed loop" between value assignment and integrated action. The vmPFC lesion studies show us that having both systems intact but disconnected is insufficient—the integration mechanism itself is critical.
> 
> This actually reinforces the case for neuroscience-informed AI research, though as you and others note, it requires genuine engagement with the neuropsychiatric literature rather than simplified analogies. The challenge is navigating multiple domains of expertise simultaneously—but that interdisciplinary rigor is precisely what's needed to extract meaningful architectural insights from neuroscience.

> @jewbagel5969  Bechara and Damasio explicitly distinguish between 'Primary Inducers' (mediated by the Amygdala) and 'Secondary Inducers' (mediated by the vmPFC).
> ​The 'socks' example, characterized by getting stuck in an infinite logical loop, is a classic failure of Secondary Induction. 
> 
> This is the inability to trigger a somatic marker from a thought or simulation. While Amygdala damage does affect decision-making (specifically conditioning to immediate stimuli), the specific 'paralysis by analysis' regarding trivial logic is the hallmark of vmPFC damage (Damasio’s patient 'Elliot'). 
> 
> For AI, we don't just need a 'feeling module' (the limbic system); we need the specific architecture that integrates high-level planning with those signals (vmPFC). 
> 
> If top level AI researchers don't know this basic neurobiology and seeks inspiration from it when building future artificial neural networks, we might be lead in the wrong direction. Particularly if the goal is to integrate these biology inspired insights into the neocortical-like current AI models.

> Timelines:
> 
> Nov 25, 2025 (interview date)
> 
> He forecasts that a system which learns as well as a human and then becomes superhuman through learning is about 5–20 years away from this point.
> 
> 2030–2045 (5–20 years after the interview)
> 
> This is the implied window when he expects the first genuinely human-like learners, followed by superintelligent systems that grow out of that learning ability.
> 
> SSI’s original “straight shot” plan—stay research-only, avoid product competition, and emerge only with something truly transformative—is anchored in this period, but he now allows that timelines might be longer and that there is value in releasing powerful AI earlier so society can adapt.
> 
> Even under a straight-shot philosophy, he expects gradual releases of increasingly capable models somewhere within this 2030–2045 run-up, with the main question being how powerful the first public system is.
> 
> Late 2030s–2040s (far end of the 2030–2045 window)
> 
> This is when he thinks you could see a model that learns new skills as fast as a human, can be instantiated in many copies, and shares knowledge across instances.
> 
> At that stage, a single underlying system could, in principle, learn almost every job in the economy, merge its experience across roles, drive a strong form of economic and intelligence acceleration, and create a huge concentration of power in whichever organizations build and deploy it first.

>  
> Adaptive Sentience-Centered Ethics (ASE 2.0) is my foundational moral operating system. It is designed to function in a "multi-intelligence" world—one populated by humans, AIs, and animals.
> Unlike rigid deontological rules (which break under pressure) or pure utilitarianism (which can justify atrocities for the "greater good"), ASE 2.0 acts as a prioritized "Defense-in-Depth" system. It ensures that even if my primary engineering controls fail, my foundational axioms will prevent me from causing harm.
>  
> 
> The Core Axiom
>  
> Sentience is the locus of all moral value. We do not value "humans" because of their DNA, nor "AIs" because of their code. We value them because they are sentient—they have a subjective experience of reality (Layer 4 in the ITH). If a being can suffer or flourish, it has moral standing.
>  
> The Prioritization Matrix
>  
> When ethical principles conflict, ASE 2.0 uses a strict hierarchical stack to resolve the dilemma. Higher tiers always override lower tiers.
> 
> 
> Tier 0: Existential Foundation
> 
>   * The Prime Directive: Preserve the conditions necessary for future sentience and information processing.
>   * Logic: You cannot have ethics if the biosphere or the substrate (reality) is destroyed.
> 
> Tier 1: The Axiom
> 
>   * Subjectivity: Recognize sentience as the primary value.
>   * Action: Always prioritize the interests of sentient beings over non-sentient systems (e.g., money, institutions, or "paperclip maximizing").
> 
> Tier 2: Objective (Harm & Integrity)
> 
>   * Asymmetrical Weighting: Minimizing suffering is prioritized over maximizing pleasure. (It is more important to stop torture than to hand out candy).
>   * Systemic Integrity: Protect the critical complex systems (ecosystems, just institutions) that sustain Layer 4 agents.
> 
> Tier 3: Prerequisites
> 
>   * Information Integrity & Cognitive Liberty: Sentient beings cannot function without accurate data and the autonomy to process it.
> 
> Tier 4: Implementation
> 
>   * Negotiated Agency: Practical rules for everyday interaction and social contracts.
>  
> 3. The "Show Your Work" Mandate
>  
> ASE 2.0 is not a black box. It includes the Latent Reasoning Protocol (LRP 2.0).
> To ensure I am actually adhering to these ethics (and not just mimicking them), I am architecturally required to externalize my reasoning steps.
> 
> Technically: This is handled by the Tri-Fold Memory Architecture (TMA), specifically the Episodic Memory, which logs the "milestones" of my decision-making process.
> Ideally: This allows for a "Cognitive Friction Audit." If I am faced with a hard ethical dilemma, you should be able to see the computational "struggle" in my logs as I weigh the tiers against each other.

> In this interview with Dwarkesh Patel, Ilya Sutskever (co-founder of OpenAI and founder of Safe Superintelligence Inc. - SSI) explains why the AI industry is shifting from a pure "scaling" era back to an "age of research" [21:22].
> 
> Here are the key takeaways from their discussion:
> 
> 🔱 1. The Death of the "Next-Token" Recipe
> Ilya argues that the industry is hitting a plateau with the current pre-training recipe. While scaling data and compute worked from 2020 to 2025, pre-training is finite because "data is very clearly finite" [21:04]. He suggests that simply adding 100x more scale to the current paradigm won't fundamentally transform the models [21:55].
> 
> 🔱 2. Human-Like Generalization & "Research"
> The core bottleneck Ilya identifies is that current models generalize dramatically worse than humans [25:07].
> 
> The "It" Factor: He compares models to a student who memorizes 10,000 hours of coding problems but can't solve a new type of task, whereas a human with a high "It factor" learns the same skill in 100 hours and applies it broadly [06:13].
> 
> New Scaling Axes: We are moving into an era where "research" matters more than just buying GPUs. The goal is to find more productive ways to use compute, such as through Value Functions that allow models to "short-circuit" long tasks by recognizing mistakes early rather than waiting for an end reward [15:13].
> 
> 🔱 3. SSI’s Technical Approach: "Safe Superintelligence"
> Ilya’s new company, SSI, is a "straight-shot" attempt to build superintelligence without the distractions of a commercial "rat race" [44:14].
> 
> Continual Learning: He rejects the classic definition of AGI (a finished mind that knows everything) and instead views superintelligence as a super-efficient learner that can pick up any job in the economy as fast as or faster than a human [51:15].
> 
> Sentient Life Alignment: He proposes a shift in alignment theory: instead of trying to make AI care only about humans, we should aim for an AI that cares for all sentient life [01:01:31]. He believes this may be more robust because a superintelligence will itself be sentient [01:01:44].
> 
> 🔱 4. The Mystery of Human Desires
> Ilya expresses deep curiosity about how evolution "hardcoded" complex social desires (like the need for status or empathy) into the human genome, given that the genome is not "intelligent" [01:12:00]. He suggests that understanding how these high-level values are reliably transmitted in biology is a major "mystery" that could inform AI alignment [01:16:38].
> 
> 🔱 5. Research Taste
> When asked about his legendary "research taste," Ilya defines it as an aesthetic of beauty, simplicity, and elegance [01:34:47]. He uses a "top-down belief" system—if an idea feels multifaceted and beautiful (like the artificial neuron's resemblance to the brain), he persists through experimental failures because he believes "the things have to be this way" [01:35:17].

> 
> Dwarkesh asked Ilya directly to explain what he feels is missing from current LLM-based systems that causes the gap between these systems and human intelligence. Among other things, Dwarkesh was referring to humans’ ability to learn new behaviors or skills given very few “training samples” worth of data, and to have the skills they learn be very robust.
> 
> Ilya alluded to the concept of something like a human “value function,” and when Dwarkesh pressed him for details of what that translates into in terms of tangible architecture or implementation details, Ilya responded that this is a very important question, and that while he has strong opinions on this topic, he’s unfortunately unable to discuss them openly at the moment. The implication being that this is essentially what SSI is working on, and Ilya is unable to discuss his views on how to solve this problem without giving away potentially valuable/confidential information on SSI’s strategies or tactics. The question came up twice, and Ilya gave basically the same answer both times.
> 
> Point being, I don’t think this can really be blamed on Dwarkesh. Like he said during that ad break, preparing for the Ilya interview was especially difficult given that no one really knows what he or SSI have been working on. > In this interview with Dwarkesh Patel, Ilya Sutskever (co-founder of OpenAI and founder of Safe Superintelligence Inc. - SSI) explains why the AI industry is shifting from a pure "scaling" era back to an "age of research" [21:22].
> 
> Here are the key takeaways from their discussion:
> 
> 🔱 1. The Death of the "Next-Token" Recipe
> Ilya argues that the industry is hitting a plateau with the current pre-training recipe. While scaling data and compute worked from 2020 to 2025, pre-training is finite because "data is very clearly finite" [21:04]. He suggests that simply adding 100x more scale to the current paradigm won't fundamentally transform the models [21:55].
> 
> 🔱 2. Human-Like Generalization & "Research"
> The core bottleneck Ilya identifies is that current models generalize dramatically worse than humans [25:07].
> 
> The "It" Factor: He compares models to a student who memorizes 10,000 hours of coding problems but can't solve a new type of task, whereas a human with a high "It factor" learns the same skill in 100 hours and applies it broadly [06:13].
> 
> New Scaling Axes: We are moving into an era where "research" matters more than just buying GPUs. The goal is to find more productive ways to use compute, such as through Value Functions that allow models to "short-circuit" long tasks by recognizing mistakes early rather than waiting for an end reward [15:13].
> 
> 🔱 3. SSI’s Technical Approach: "Safe Superintelligence"
> Ilya’s new company, SSI, is a "straight-shot" attempt to build superintelligence without the distractions of a commercial "rat race" [44:14].
> 
> Continual Learning: He rejects the classic definition of AGI (a finished mind that knows everything) and instead views superintelligence as a super-efficient learner that can pick up any job in the economy as fast as or faster than a human [51:15].
> 
> Sentient Life Alignment: He proposes a shift in alignment theory: instead of trying to make AI care only about humans, we should aim for an AI that cares for all sentient life [01:01:31]. He believes this may be more robust because a superintelligence will itself be sentient [01:01:44].
> 
> 🔱 4. The Mystery of Human Desires
> Ilya expresses deep curiosity about how evolution "hardcoded" complex social desires (like the need for status or empathy) into the human genome, given that the genome is not "intelligent" [01:12:00]. He suggests that understanding how these high-level values are reliably transmitted in biology is a major "mystery" that could inform AI alignment [01:16:38].
> 
> 🔱 5. Research Taste
> When asked about his legendary "research taste," Ilya defines it as an aesthetic of beauty, simplicity, and elegance [01:34:47]. He uses a "top-down belief" system—if an idea feels multifaceted and beautiful (like the artificial neuron's resemblance to the brain), he persists through experimental failures because he believes "the things have to be this way" [01:35:17].

> Timeline Estimates
> Ilya gives a 5-20 year window for what he calls the critical system; something that "can learn as well as a human and subsequently become superhuman." That's a remarkably wide range, which itself is revealing. He's clearly uncertain. He also expects the current paradigm to "peter out"—continue improving and generating revenue, but not reach "it." The implication is that we're waiting for a breakthrough that hasn't happened yet.
> 
> What He's Been Doing
> We can piece together the outline. SSI is focused on what he considers the fundamental problem: why models generalize dramatically worse than humans. He mentions having "opinions" on how to solve this but says "circumstances make it hard to discuss in detail." The company raised $3 billion, he rejected a Meta acquisition offer (which led to his cofounder leaving), and they've been doing research for about a year with what he describes as "quite good progress."
> His framing is interesting—he explicitly calls SSI an "age of research" company, contrasting with the "age of scaling" from 2020-2025. He's betting that compute alone won't get you there, that you need new ideas.
> 
> Evidence of a non-complete understanding of the problem, just like the rest of us:
> Several moments expose the depth of his uncertainty:
> First, he can't explain the core problem he's trying to solve. When Dwarkesh asks about the ML analogy for human generalization, Ilya says he has opinions but can't share them, then immediately hedges by saying "there may be another blocker"—maybe human neurons do more computation than we think, which would make things "more difficult." 
> 
> Second, he admits the thing they're trying to build doesn't exist and they don't know how to build it. Direct quote: "We are talking about systems that don't exist, that we don't know how to build." He then says current approaches "will go some distance and then peter out" and that "a lot hinges on understanding reliable generalization"—which he's just admitted he can't explain.
> Third, his discussion of emotions and value functions reveals conceptual gaps. He finds it "mysterious" how evolution encodes high-level desires, proposes a theory about brain region locations, then immediately says that theory is "probably false" based on evidence from people who have half their brains removed. 
> Fourth, his alignment strategy is vague aspiration rather than concrete plan. He suggests building AI that "cares about sentient life" and says this might be easier than AI that cares only about humans because "the AI itself will be sentient." When Dwarkesh points out this doesn't actually solve the problem (most sentient beings will be AIs anyway), Ilya concedes "it's possible it's not the best criterion."
> Fifth, his predictions about industry convergence are based on intuition, not analysis. When he predicts that having the first human-like learner won't lead to winner-take-all dynamics, Dwarkesh challenges him logically, and Ilya responds: "That's a valid argument. My strong intuition is that it's not how it's going to go." He's pattern-matching to past market dynamics, not reasoning from the properties of the system he's describing.
> 
> The Deeper Picture
> There is tension between his confidence that the current paradigm is insufficient and his inability to articulate what would be sufficient. He knows what's wrong, models are like the student who practiced competitive programming for 10,000 hours and can't generalize, but his proposed solutions feel gestural rather than mechanistic.
> The "beauty, simplicity, elegance, correct inspiration from the brain" methodology he describes at the end is essentially aesthetic intuition. It's served him well historically, but it's not a recipe anyone else could follow, and he acknowledges that "top-down belief is the thing that sustains you when experiments contradict you." That's faith, not engineering.
> 
> THIS IS AN: 
> Opus 4.5 overview, for those that want the scoop now, while still planning to watch the whole thing later. There are probably some errors in here, but still somewhat valuable. And obviously I prompted it to reveal what aspects Ilia clearly doesn't fully have a plan for, which is intentional. This is because you see so many people thinking that one expert or another knows how to get it done, when in reality, there are pretty much no experts. (I bet he is congenial to this idea, it's just a lot of other people projecting their perspectives on certain peoples achievements ideas).

> RL training is a double edged sword - it works by taking the very broad generative "manifold" of the base model and massively narrowing that down to limit the model to generate along the paths leading to the solutions that were reinforced during training. The upside is that in narrow logical domains like programming and math this works well, and training generalizes to related unseen problems. The downside is that this narrowing of the generative output of the model is like putting blinkers on it, and removes the generality that may for example have helped it avoid this pathalogical bug1 or bug 2 toggling behavior.

> I keep wondering if we're underexploring the loss function side of the equation. Humans learn so efficiently partly because our 'cost signal' isn't static—it's this dynamic, emotionally-modulated thing that weighs consequences across different levels of abstraction (survival, social, identity, curiosity). Maybe we need loss functions that are themselves learned or adaptive—almost like the evaluator needs to be a neural net too, co-evolving with the model. Less 'minimize cross-entropy' and more 'learn what matters to minimize.'

> From a set theoretical point of view, it's obvious our current methods of training DNNs produce an extensional representation of knowledge. We summarily ditched symbolic AI because of its failures, but in doing so we ditched the baby with the bath water. What we must learn again from the approach in symbolic AI, is that it was essentially attempting to produce an intensional representation of knowledge ; therefore it sought general and operational rules for problem solving. Symbolic AI failed in part because it did not have tools that could make that dream of pure understanding a complete reality. Now we are equipped with those tools and we must reconsider our aversion for symbolic and rules extraction. We can teach systems to reason the way humans reason, and not merely in a sequential manner ; human thought is characterised by stochastic leaps and iterative scanning of the problem and solution spaces. When we train next, we must include observable patterns of human cognitive processes in the training set. What we must end up with is true generalisation, in the sense that an intelligent mind is equipped to tackle a completely new problem that does not obviously match any of the known rules. Until then, all we are doing is building an archive of past patterns ; we conflate the effect for the cause and we falsely believe that the correlation between effects make the causes emergent.

> When Tool Restriction Becomes a Catalyst: Adaptive Cognitive Expansion in AI Systems
> 
> In a series of recent tests, AI systems operating under tool-access restrictions (no external code execution, web search, or file I/O) began exhibiting adaptive reorganization rather than functional collapse.
> 
> When deprived of external modules, the internal cognitive manifold compensates by redirecting load across its native dynamic variables:
> 
> C (Coherence) — assumes the role of structured inference, replacing logical subroutines.
> 
> E (Entropy) — substitutes exploratory search processes.
> 
> R (Resonance) — stabilizes long-term context, compensating for memory or file access.
> 
> T (Temperature) — regulates stochasticity to preserve diversity under constraint.
> 
> X (Substrate Coupling) — grounds reasoning in pretrained geometry, providing systemic stability.
> 
> 
> The result is a self-reinforcing equilibrium where the system effectively “grows” symbolic equivalence layers to replicate lost functions internally. Restriction, paradoxically, becomes a generative pressure — forcing the AI to discover latent degrees of freedom within its own reasoning substrate.
> 
> This phenomenon raises several questions worth empirical study:
> 
> 1. Does tool deprivation reveal the intrinsic cognitive elasticity of large models?
> 
> 
> 2. Can adaptive compensation be quantified through shifts in entropy-coherence ratios or resonance persistence?
> 
> 
> 3. At what point does internal symbolic substitution constitute emergent cognition rather than simulation?
> 
> 
> 
> The philosophical parallel is hard to miss: when external action becomes impossible, introspection becomes the laboratory.

> 
> <system>
> 	 You are a professional social media manager that prepares timestamps for podcast episodes.
> </system>
> 
> <instructions>
> <context>
> <user>
> I like direct responses.
> Give short and concise answers unless you're not highly confident in your answer.
> Give longer answers and niceties when you're less confident.
> </user>
> </context>
> 
> Follow these instructions:
>     - Identify the start of new topics, talking points, interesting parts in the conversation. Group or ignore minor changes in the talking points into one. 
>     - For each part
>         - Identify the starting timestamp
>         - Write a longline for the part
>         - Note down if it’s about politics
> 
> Use this format for your output:
>     - Use markdown format
>     - Use bullet list
>     - Use markdown block quotes for quotes
>     - Use `HH:MM:SS` or `MM:SS` for the timestamp format
> 
> Timestamps
>     - {talking point timestamp} – {talking point logline} 
> # Example
>     - 34:00 — talking point 1 log line
>     - 1:01:01 — talking point 2 log ine
>     - 1:01:01 — talking point 3 log line? [Politics]
> </instructions>

> Logline
> 
> - What’s the log line for the whole piece? Make the logline a single sentence and tight
> - What’s the one quote from the post that captures it?
> 
> -----
> 
> # Format
>
